speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 to ask leave to move a motion on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. In view of the government's appalling lack of concern with respect to health research in Canada as elaborated in the remarks of Nobel Prize winner Dr. Gerhard Herzberg at the recent conference of Canadians for Health Research, and having regard to the stress laid by Dr. Herzberg on the need for the better funding of health research, 1 move, seconded by the hon. member for Oxford (Mr. Halliday):
That the government take action to bring health research in this country up to international standards so that Canadians may enjoy healthier and longer lives.

speechtext:

That Canada adopt a long term beef import policy and that as soon as possible parliament enact legislation to regulate the importation of beef, veal and live slaughter-cattle.

Commerce): I am rapidly becoming aware of the Broadbent statistics.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the obligation and the duty for elected representatives to intervene periodically and more officially in this House have been today vested in me. I express my gratitude to the Prime Minister for the confidence he thus places in me. All citizens in Compton riding also appreciate that mark of confidence regarding their desire to make the reality known to all Canada, unfortunate though it may be.
326

October 27, 1977
The Address-Mr. Tessier
Those preoccupations and the avenue open to them today would appear sterile and outrageous for some 70,000 of my fellow citizens from the province of Quebec if they endorsed without question the position of the government and particularly of the party to which I belong.
Would anyone dare presume of my convictions regarding my chief, my colleagues, my allegiance? I do not think so. Mr. Speaker, even if my modest contribution to the ideal we are striving for were in the denunciation of its weaknesses, I would be convinced to have honestly contributed and offered what I have left of sincerity as member of a party and as a member of the institution of the Parliament of Canada.
Compton riding would figure favourably in a global analysis of the situation in Quebec on the cultural, social and economic aspects. The population of Compton is 80 per cent Francophone and 20 per cent Anglophone. The level of unemployment is one of the highest in the country and we have no hope of an economic recovery as our economy has long been in a state of stagnation. The existing industry steadily curtails its operations and it seems almost impossible to get new markets.
The direct allusion made by Her Majesty in her Speech from the Throne concerning the imminence of feelings like alienation, hostility and resentment caused by a possible lack of stability and equity is now part of day-to-day reactions in my riding.
Mr. Speaker, although I loudly voice my appreciation, this does not mean that 1 do not endorse the views of hundreds of my fellow-citizens who fight constantly against the departure of our young people, the phasing out and reduction of our essential services such as rail transportation and even the postal services in some cases. Among other things and with the help of the federal government those generous citizens promoted a tourist resort in Coaticook and an outdoor recreational area in Lake Megantic that are practically unique in Quebec as regards their location and their size.
It is with satisfaction as well that I welcome the recent action taken by a few businessmen and some 360 factory workers to preserve Waterville's source of livelihood and its right to work. It is a perfect example that enables me to reassert my confidence in private enterprises while urging the government to support equitably.
Mr. Speaker, like most hon. members, I cannot dissociate the Speech from the Throne from the economic and fiscal statement of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien). In fact, both statements appear to me as related and complementary.
The federal government can only prove its good intentions by showing positively and unequivocally its will to stimulate our economy as a whole. What about the proposals put forward by the Minister of Finance? Although commendable, do they really take into account the prime purpose, which is to establish an adequate infrastructure for the creation of permanent jobs? Unfortunately, we cannot overlook the three factors which, as the Minister of Finance stated, hinder our growth- the relative weakness of our export markets, the high cost of

our production, mainly due to ever increasing wage demands, and the loss of confidence brought about by our slow growth and the political uncertainty resulting from our threatened national unity.
I recognize that these problems are not peculiar to our country. However, whereas experts are considering development models for some third world countries, we fail to take in our country a systematic approach to strengthen our own economic structure, and this often under the pretence that we are rich and that our per capita income is higher than that of most other nations.
Mr. Speaker, the constituency of Compton wants to express today its dissatisfaction at the failure or incapacity of existing formulas to meet its need to survive economically. The problem lies in the incapacity of the government to conceive the existence of the rural environment. And yet, it exists and many feel that it offers some characteristics likely to facilitate the planning of tomorrow's society. There more than anywhere else, the physical and human environment still conveys our sense of belonging and our desire to participate in the social development of our community.
Should I stress officially the necessity of creating a department of rural development or some other body-the kind that our fathers called, quite rightly, the department of colonization, even though this term is now somewhat obsolete and has a bad connotation-at the risk of being taxed with disrespect in the history of our country of which we claim to be the actors? Of course, bureaucracy does not put up very well with such a justification, but you will agree with me that Canada means more than Montreal or Toronto and that non-metropolitan areas now provide the best conditions in which to attain our goals of social and economic development.
While Montreal is overpopulated and congested, East Angus is losing its people, with the danger of becoming a depressed area. The pulp and paper industry, one of the biggest sores in the constituency of Compton, needs the federal government to take an immediate stand. In that respect, the Quebec scheme seems to me to be very well thought out, and even our serene silence itself is no longer acceptable. The federal government must take a sensible and courageous position. Consultation between the various parties involved in this debate is both desirable and needed. The federal authorities have the legal right to act. Let us therefore recognize our clear responsibility to the thousands of workers who gave up as much as 40 years of their lives, only to fall victims of our silence at 55.
On the other hand, the textile industry is entitled to the protective measures announced in December 76 by the then Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, Mr. Chretien. In a joint release issued last week, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) announced that negotiations would be held on bilateral protective agreements for a three-year period. That industry wished that the extension of those protective measures be immediately confirmed, so that they may go ahead and plan their production and marketing resources on a sound basis. This is not too much to ask in order to ensure the
October 27, 1977

stability of this vital sector of the economy of Compton and the Eastern Townships as a whole.
Mr. Speaker, the reference in the throne speech to the food industry warrants special attention. I have a duty to focus on it in view of the agricultural nature of my constituency and my awareness that the federal government will have very delicate responsibilities to assume in the coming months. 1 also have a conviction that certain farming groups will be listening to my remarks as much as they did to the simple reference in the throne speech to certain actions. I am also certain that my remarks will inform the government of certain facts, and such information will no doubt cause controversy among those mainly concerned.
Mr. Speaker, we must welcome a policy promoting agricultural development through a better utilization of our food industry's capacity. I also endorse any initiative to promote the convening of a national food conference in order to develop a strategy for the Canadian food sector. Such a conference will also insist on better information of producers, consumers and processors. It should also give renewed significance to a balanced representation at the marketing board level.
This, however, leads me to question certain apprehensions. They have to do with the role and the status of farm producers themselves, and any initiative by the federal government will have to be based on consultation with them. Here is why: they are the ones producing and the government must make sure they get a fair return for that production.
Our agricultural sector is considered as one to be copied by several other producing countries. I was myself informed during the consultations at Brussels of the envy felt by certain member countries of the European Community, and I would like here, Mr. Speaker, to elaborate on those doubts I expressed a moment ago. They have to do with the Canadian dairy policy. It would be regrettable indeed if a reputation so dearly acquired should be tarnished by a malaise that is now being felt by the government and the producers themselves.
In that sense, I do admit that some readjustments are necessary in the very short run, otherwise open pressures would be warranted to have a public inquiry carried out on the administration and publication of marketing quotas for the next four years. It seems obvious on this day that very questionable practices have crept into the distribution of those quotas and that those responsible for such an usurpation- often producers representatives themselves-are causing enormous financial harm to the majority of those producers whose honesty however is unquestioned. The awareness of that breach of right is starting to poison the relationships between the producers and the federal government, and that, Mr. Speaker, is unacceptable. The cause of the malaise is identified and that is the most relevant reason for having such an inquiry and at least the need to rethink the membership of the supply management committee. The principle of equity will then have to underly that required operation in terms of producers representation.
That will result in a more vigilant awareness of producers with respect to their official organizations and the dangers
The Address-Mr. Tessier
inherent in such a system, however democratic it may be, will be better controlled. It would be regrettable indeed, Mr. Speaker, if after blaming us for everything the producers were to start accusing one another.
These are my precise views on the matters which we should discuss within the next months. National unity requires that all our efforts be directed to implementing decent measures to insure stability and equity in the economy of Canada and to guarantee the support of the population of Compton riding in an eventual consultation on the benefits to Quebec of its participation in the Canadian political evolution. It is absolutely necessary that the federal government protect the integrity of Canada and propose, as I mentioned, concrete amendments to answer legitimate rights and feasible aspirations of the Quebecers, and of all other provinces.

Mr. Speaker, all the frustrations generated by three centuries of cultural confusion in Quebec make it more than ever necessary for all levels of government to approach this issue with an open and understanding mind. The political development of this beloved country of ours requires a positive attitude as well as ready acceptance of a reality that is challenging us, both as members of parliament and as private citizens. What are the solutions? There are some inasmuch as the very foundations of Canadian unity will be perceived as concrete realities by the Canadian people. In this matter, it is up to the federal government to substantiate or refute the views of those who question the basis of confederation. In trying to justify its existence, the federal government should not simply argue that it is the living symbol of the Canadian nation. Instead of indulging in such sophistry, it should endeavour to demonstrate the respective merits of centralization versus decentralization and account for its past and present policies. In this sense, cooperation between the federal and provincial secretariats appears essential in order to clarify or avoid the dualism which is at the root of our recent political evolution now being in jeopardy.
The present situation offers us the choice between several options, but it should not in any case justify our absence from several frontlines on which we are being attacked. It is imperative that immediate formulas provide for a louder presence of the various caucuses of Parliament in order to weaken a political strategy through which certain political authorities in Quebec intend to influence public opinion and try to make us appear as unable to consider any kind of changes.
Mr. Speaker, the present circumstances and the Speech from the Throne invite us to affirm clearly our presence as the spokesmen for a way of being which is indispensable to reach the objectives which the post-war generation has set for itself, a passionate generation to which I belong and whose need for clear-cut solutions I echo. One can therefore deduct from this affirmation that our young people should have a say in the coming decisions which will affect them. It is a legitimate

I am not so enthusiastic about the contents of the speech. When I say that, I believe I am voicing the opinion of a great many people in Canada.
I congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) on accepting the criticism and pressure put on government by many Canadians with regard to the iniquitous legislation which would have taxed life insurance proceeds. I received a great deal of mail condemning that proposal. Had that legislation been passed, we would have been the only country in the world taxing the proceeds of life insurance. It would have meant robbing the widows and orphans. I congratulate the government on that.
The government has finally recognized that the average Canadian is highly overtaxed. I do not know how many millions of dollars are involved, but tax reductions of $100 are

being given to the ordinary taxpayers. This amounts to a little under $2 a week. It is a small enough amount, but at least it is a step in the right direction. But to pretend that it is a solution to our great economic problems is absolutely ridiculous. Canadians are fed up. They do not want handouts or shortterm goodies. Why does the government not come up with serious solutions to end this economic uncertainty? The opinion of a great many people is that it is afraid to do that. The Minister of Finance made ever so slight suggestions that mistakes have been made in the past. Let's call a spade a spade. The Liberal government is responsible for the miserable state of our economy.
The latest depressing sequel to this economic mess is massive layoffs at INCO plants in Sudbury, Thompson, Manitoba, in the constituency of the hon. member for Churchill (Mr. Smith), and Port Colborne. This will have drastic effects on the economies in those areas. I hope that something can be done to save those jobs which are so important not only to the workers and their families, but to the entire community.
Down through the years the government has provided assistance to big business. Certainly assistance to many businesses is necessary. I do not believe you have to put all your eggs in one basket. We should not put our entire faith and all our resources at the disposal of big business. We should give more assistance to small business. Small business provides 60 per cent of the jobs, the majority of jobs in this country. It accounts for more than 50 per cent of the value of business that is generated. I believe our gross national product is in the neighbourhood of $200 billion. I am sure most members will agree that this vital part of our economy was virtually ignored in the Speech from the Throne as well as in the minibudget which the Minister of Finance presented to the House last Thursday.
We do not have an overall policy dealing with small business and the problems relating to it. The United States has a very significant program geared to small business. Those who were in the House last week when our spokesman for small business participated in the debate heard the hon. member for High Park-Humber Valley (Mr. Jelinek) spell out the suggestions which the Conservative party recommends to assist small business.
As a rural member of parliament, I received innumerable calls from small businessmen. This morning I received a call from a businessman asking about the advantageous interest rates on small business loans. According to the government, this is something wonderful. It was extolled by the previous Minister of Finance. However, when it comes down to the cold, hard facts, when you are in the office of the bank manager, the advantageous rates for small business loans seem to be far off in never, never land. I hope the government will do something in this session to ensure that money is available to small business establishments at reasonable rates.
I believe that the rates of the Federal Business Development Bank are down slightly. This businessman who called me this morning had a $25,000 loan approved and processed a year ago at 12 per cent. He is trying to get the interest rate
October 27, 1977

adjusted. I assume that under his contract he is locked into a 12 per cent rate for the duration of the loan. When interest rates come down, the Federal Business Development Bank should be able to adjust rates to assist the small businessman. That is certainly worthy of consideration and, 1 hope, approval.
The Minister of Finance was pre-empted by the Prime Minister with regard to the $150 million that is to be pumped into the economy. We are still not clear how this will be administered and who will receive it. In a statement today, the Minister of Finance said it was going to certain departments. There has been much talk about the auto pact. From Canada's point of view, we are now an importer of auto parts.
I am aware that the auto pact is a two-way street. There have been many heated questions, including today, on this very important segment of our economy.
Despite the fact that 1 represent the paradise vacationland of Canada, Parry Sound-Muskoka, there are some very good industries in my constituency. There are two plants which provide auto parts for the various automobile companies. One plant in particular is not a small plant trying to survive without any funds or assets. It is a branch of Rockwell International and is located in Parry Sound. Word has gone out that the staff of that plant is to be cut by more than 50 per cent, from 220 to 100. This is very serious in an area where there is a small population. The Rockwell plant was a corporate citizen.
I had the privilege of meeting with municipal officials as well as officials of the plant. The facts they presented were shocking. I am sure many members will be interested in this. In the past five years, this plant has been faced with huge increases. Hydro has increased by 128 per cent. Five years ago they paid $8,000 a month; now, it is $14,000. Canada Pension Plan premiums have increased by 79 per cent; costs due to strikes and accidents have risen by 190 per cent and labour costs by 133 per cent. They ask: How can we compete successfully in the face of increases like this and keep the plant functioning at full capacity?

Mr. Speaker, I am thrilled to speak during the debate on the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne, especially since Her Majesty herself delivered the speech.
Mr. Speaker, we could have expected on that occasion that the Speech from the Throne would be more substantial and show some maturity on the part of Parliament in general and the government in particular. Unfortunately, I think that it was a lost opportunity to make something interesting and original. On the contrary, it can be said that we heard the same trivia delivered in a royal fashion.
Mr. Speaker, within the present Canadian context it is extremely important that hon. members in this House cast aside their prejudices, parochialism and overcome their bitterness and disappointments. The time has come for us to demonstrate our maturity and serenity and try to resolve problems which are assuming crisis proportions.
Mr. Speaker, we must realize that, unfortunately, this government does not seem to have yet accepted the choice the province of Quebec made about a year ago. Cabinet members, starting from the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) himself, vent their bitterness and resentment and I am afraid,
October 27, 1977

and this is very serious, they are even trying to hinder the work of the Quebec government. Mr. Speaker, this is not mature behaviour. It is irresponsible and childish. On the election night, last year, we heard all kinds of poppycock by the Prime Minister and the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Lessard) who went so far as to say: You will not get any more money in Quebec. That will teach you how to behave. After they got that off their chests, you could expect they would calm down and get off Quebec's back whether they liked its government or not.
Mr. Speaker, a year has now passed. It seems to me they should have regained their composure by now but they have not. And we saw the Prime Minister try a bit of brinkmanship and go down to Washington where he, a man credited with a high intellect, did something quite stupid: he said that Quebec independence was a crime against mankind. Mr. Speaker, what an irresponsible statement! It is going overboard! It is a total lack of respect for Canada. Yet he did not stop there. In the Speech from the Throne he decides on a referendum war. There will be a referendum and a cross-referendum. The Prime Minister will make people in Quebec and the rest of Canada say whatever he wants them to say. Where is his sense of responsibility, Mr. Speaker? When will our good friends opposite cease to equate red-blooded patriots with people bent on the destruction of our country?
Mr. Speaker, it is a falsehood. When our friends opposite claim that the hon. member for Champlain and the Quebec government and people are separatists they are making malicious allegations. As far as I know the Quebec government and the hon. member for Champlain feel the way the Socred M.P.s demonstrated they felt last week end. They want to live in harmony in this country. They want the real, concrete groups which make up this country to live their own lives and shape their own futures.
There is therefore nothing negative about the decision made by Quebecers last year. Why is the government taking such an attitude? Would it be, Mr. Speaker, to try to hide the enormous weaknesses in the economy? Would it be to make people forget about unemployment? Would it be to hide inflation? Would it be to make people forget the incompetence of cabinet members? Mr. Speaker, we may well wonder when we see a prime minister over-react and fight windmills like Don Quixote.
Mr. Speaker, as far as I know, the Parti Quebecois now in power in Quebec only said that it wanted a new agreement in Canada, that it wanted a new partnership based this time on the elementary justice principle of true equality. What is wrong with that? What is so wrong that we should go and say in Washington that it is a crime against humanity? Mr. Speaker, let us be calm and let us see things as they really are. Why should we want to convey a false impression to those who do not want Canada to survive, because if it does, it will be once again thanks to the spirit of Quebecers who until now have acted as a sort of buffer, as a catalyst to prevent Canada from being simply a geographic extension of the United States. We no longer want to play such a secondary role. We want a

positive role. We want to assert ourselves as we are. That is why, in my opinion, Quebec is now able to show the way towards the implementation of this new Canada, a Canada restructured according to everybody's needs, a Canada where everyone will be truly free to develop to one's liking, a Canada where there will finally be true equality, a Canada where there will no longer be absurdities as there now are.
I was listening the other day to the Minister of Communications (Mrs. Sauve). Why should the taxes of Rene Matte, member of parliament for Champlain, Quebec taxpayer, who is in perfect agreement with the Quebec government, be used to bring charges against me? We have been masochistic long enough without this. I was listening to the hon. member for Hull (Mr. Isabelle) yesterday. What he said was terrible. Perhaps the hon. member for Compton (Mr. Tessier) had him in mind when he said that Quebec members are a "gang of nobodies". Mr. Speaker, I did not say that. The hon. member for Compton is reported as having said, and I quote:
As he stated in his document of last July, Mr. Tessier maintained yesterday that Quebec Liberal members have never taken the necessary steps to improve their image or to put forward Quebec's views.
Mr. Speaker, if there was no development in Hull, it is because some members, like the present member for Hull, have always managed to prevent development from taking place on both sides of the Ottawa river. I find he considers the federal government and the Parliament buildings in Ottawa as an umbrella, as a kind of Santa Claus. This hon. member is rather late, Mr. Speaker, whereas since Quebecers have decided on their own to bend down on their knees no longer, to creep no longer, they have decided to hold hands with the rest of Canada and to say from now on: Let us give this country a real striking force which will be held as an example throughout the world. At noon I asked a question of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) and the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner). Mr. Speaker, in the very region which the Minister of Finance represents a company has just laid off some 300 to 400 workers. What has the federal government done to prevent Wayagamack from closing down? What has it

The Address-Mr. Matte
done? Nothing, because it would be quite pleased to see this company close down. It would be quite pleased to see Quebec at grips with an even higher unemployment rate, and then tell the people: Do not go off on your own, just see what will happen if you do! You will go bankrupt!
Mr. Speaker, such a behaviour is terrible. Somebody must denounce it. It is terrible, but that is what they are doing. So, the Minister of Finance who represents the riding of Saint-Maurice, 10 miles away from Wayagamack, prefers not to do anything in order to prove to the people in Quebec that they made a bad choice in the last election. It is shocking, but that's the way it is, Mr. Speaker.
And the threats made by the regional economic expansion minister (Mr. Lessard) are carried out. They will not save Quebec, and above all they do not want things to run smoothly in Quebec. What is one to think of people who act this way, Mr. Speaker? What is one to think of people like the Minister of Communications (Mrs. Sauve) who also said, in order to prove that Quebecers all agree with the federal government and disagree with the Quebec government: In my riding, I have distributed 5,000 gadgets? Puzzles, Mr. Speaker, when I am considered a separatist. Good heavens, give us puzzles! Everybody also likes that in my constituency. Are we now to base our policies on gadgets and to determine what the people in Quebec want according to the distribution of gadgets? What a poor argument!
Mr. Speaker, since a solution has to be found to a global problem, let us stop the name-calling and let us start being positive. Maybe our party views the matter differently from the party now in power in Quebec, but it all comes to the same thing. We want all the provinces to consider completely renewing the Confederation, so that we may first negotiate an association on equal terms. If that does not work, we will fully agree to independence. Maybe the Parti Quebecois views this from another point of view because they say: First we become independent and then form an association. That is the only difference between our party and the Parti Quebecois.
From now on, Mr. Speaker, it must be known that our goal is simply to restructure Canada as we really want it to be, without being unfair to anybody, by creating a healthy climate instead of being mean or imputing motives to others.
And then, we will no longer have committees which we want to be unbiased while they are not. Every time I hear about committees on Canadian unity, I wonder what it means, in terms of what Canadian unity is related to the Prime Minister's conception of it. Is there anything wrong with a Canadian unity that would involve five areas where sovereign states would agree to draft a new constitution, where each would freely determine the fields that must be shared, which ones should not be affected?
Mr. Speaker, if we were sensible enough to reflect on such matters, we would see why this government is trying to create trouble where there is none. In yesterday's paper, there is a report of what Mr. Levesque said in British Columbia:

Mr. Levesque stated that he favours a proposal whereby a Canada made up of five partners each representing one large area of the country would negotiate a new form of Confederation.
Mr. Speaker, far from being against the confederative principle, I should like Canada to become a real confederacy, that is to say a union of sovereign states. We should not forget something very important. Of course there are other issues, but because this includes all the others, I do not mind devoting some time to it. The necessity to deal objectively with this issue stems from the fact that the future of our country depends on it. If, from the point of view of history, Quebec insists on being considered as a separate entity, as a nation, nobody can blame it. If it can help Ontario adopt similar views for itself, why not make Ontario independent as well? Why not make the Prairies independent? Why not make British Columbia and the Maritimes independent? And with these five independent entities, we could build a marvelous and diversified Canada, yes, an harmonious Canada where it would be nice to live and where there would be no subordinates.
As far as I know, Mr. Speaker, the purpose of such a proposal, far from seeking the destruction of our country, is to make it greater and progress still further. We shall achieve this purpose only if we realize the need to deal objectively with this issue, and later with other issues, such as the economy and social affairs. This is something important and urgent, Mr. Speaker, but it is a fact that Quebecers will no longer agree to go where the money is and forget about such things as pride and dignity, for I shall make a point of telling Quebecers and making them understand that wealth is the reward of pride and dignity.

Mr. Speaker, the responsibilities of the Secretary of State are a little like a cafeteria; there is an enormous range of responsibilities, including official languages policy, protocol, state funerals and education. There are a variety of things I could speak about this afternoon, and I would like to speak about them all, but given the time constraints I will concentrate my remarks on the responsibilities I have in relation to official languages policy.
There is a very marked difference of view between the government and the official opposition in relation to official languages. The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) regards two official languages in Canada as a divisive force within our country, almost a millstone around our necks, or at best, to be fair to him, he regards them as a regrettable necessity. We on the government side, on the contrary, regard our two official languages as an opportunity, something to be welcomed and something to be made a real and vital force in our society which will strengthen a distinctive Canadian identity.
The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) pretends that the official languages policy has been a cause of the present tensions in our country. That view of his is the reverse of the
October 27, 1977

truth. Of course there have been some errors in implementation, but by far the majority of our efforts have been successful. That is not merely the view of the government; that is the view, as well, of Mr. Spicer, the former Commissioner of Official Languages, who indicated that, in spite of some criticism, 80 per cent of our efforts were useful and successful. Nor, as the Leader of the Opposition would have us believe, are the forces of separation simply a reflection of Canada's economic problems. I do not minimize for a moment the importance of the economic challenges to this country-challenges to governments, to management and workers alike. But to believe that solving these economic problems will in itself lead to the end of the thrust for separation is either wilful misrepresentation or simple-minded innocence verging on irresponsibility.
The roots of separation in Quebec are much more complicated than that simple-minded analysis. The forces for separation have increased despite unprecedented prosperity in our country over the past 15 years. The thrust for separation reflects more than anything else a sense of insecurity, whether justified or not, and pessimism over the ability of the French language and culture not simply to survive but to thrive in a North American society which modern technology and communications make more and more complex and integrated.

We will succeed in staying the forces working for separation only if we can honestly say to French Canadians that one of our ultimate goals is to see to it that throughout Canada a climate proper to the development of French language and culture will prevail. And if Anglophones cannot find in themselves enough generosity to work toward this goal, if we cannot honestly give them this assurance, then Canada's days are numbered. The Leader of the Opposition did not understand that, and he takes a negative and pernicious approach on official languages.

I mentioned earlier that there has been a substantial measure of success in our official languages policy and its implementation. Nevertheless, all members of the House will recognize that this policy has continued to be the object of some large degree of misunderstanding on the part of certain sections of the Canadian public. In the face of this, the government felt it necessary to review its policies and develop a new expression of the proposals that have guided its actions in relation to official languages over the past ten years.
The newly expressed principles formed the core of the document "A National Understanding" which outlines the kind of relationship that must exist between Francophones and Anglophones in this country, a relationship based on equality. The document sets out in clear terms the basic principles that, taken together, constitute the official languages policy of Canada. It is the purpose of these principles to give concrete expression to the equality of status of English and French as the official languages of Canada. It is the hope of the federal government that these principles will be accepted by all Canadians and by the provincial governments, in order to
The Address-Mr. Roberts
safeguard the fundamental linguistic duality of Canada within the framework of its cultural diversity.
With this in mind, the federal government has reassessed its own situation in the public service and, given the progress made to date in providing services in both official languages, is now in a position to implement the gradual elimination of the special language training efforts in the public service, expecting that the educational system will thereafter provide the necessary bilingual candidates to meet its needs.
The emphasis that must be given to this area gives special importance to the negotiation of new education arrangements with the provinces which are presently under way. Let me add that those negotiations are not merely a recent response to the problem. Over the past decade, for about seven years the government has provided something like two-thirds of $1 billion to provincial governments to assist them in expanding their school systems for second and minority language education. We are concerned that the present negotiations make the objectives of the agreements more precise and establish criteria and methods of evaluation so that all levels of government may be aware of the degree of success of our joint efforts.
But I should make one thing clear. The federal government does not regard the efforts of the provinces in this area as a special concession or favour to the federal government. They are, rather, a response to the needs of the citizens of their provinces, and it is exactly the purpose of our statement in "A National Understanding" to urge the provincial governments to accept for themselves the application of official languages policy within their own areas of jurisdiction, including education.
We have all been encouraged by the response of the provincial premiers at their conference this summer in St. Andrews, New Brunswick where they committed themselves to working out ways of improving the educational facilities available to French-language citizens across Canada. We await the results of their studies with considerable interest and optimism.
I referred a few moments ago to the passage of the Official Languages Act. That was a crucial step. Those who argue that our official languages policy has been a cause of division in this country should pause for one moment and reflect honestly on what the situation would be if we had not undertaken this commitment. Assuredly, Mr. Speaker, we would not now be agonizing over keeping this country together. Failure to have embarked on the official languages policy would have torn the country apart long before this.
The Official Languages Act has stood the test of time well. There are, however, we believe, useful changes that could be made to it to reinforce its effectiveness. I shall, therefore, be presenting to the House amendments which will, especially, strengthen the powers of the Commissioner of Official Languages.

We will see to it that the Commissioner of Official Languages, who is a representative of Parliament and has the

October 27, 1977
The Address-Mr. Roberts
support of Parliament, can in the shortest possible time apply the principles of the official languages policy established by Parliament.
The situation of the official language minority groups in Canada is another area of very special concern. Every Canadian who has at heart the future of Confederation really must recognize how important it is to ensure in fact the survival of the official language minority groups, and their survival and development not as isolated enclaves but rather as integral parts of life in Canada. I am of course referring to the French-speaking minorities outside Quebec and English-speaking minorities in Quebec.
Our government really wants to see that French and English minorities get fair and equitable treatment and not be regarded as second-class citizens.
As for the French-speaking minority groups, last spring the government received a revealing report entitled "Lord Durham's Heirs". The study recommended many steps which could be taken to ensure real survival of Francophone groups outside Quebec. The government studied that document in very great detail.
After consultation with the hon. members who are the legitimate spokesmen of Francophone minorities outside Quebec, I intend to announce what the federal government proposes to do to serve them well. 1 trust I can hold those consultations within a month and, therefore, announce within a few weeks what new measures we intend to take.
Most of the recommendations contained in the report "Lord Durham's Heirs" apply to provincial and municipal governments. That is why, in fact, the government has suggested an amendment to the constitution, in line with the proposal made last month, in the field of education, to the provincial premiers, and also in line with the Victoria charter with regard to other aspects of the rights recognized in conjunction with the official languages. That would be the surest way of achieving our objectives. If Anglophone provinces see the need for amending our constitution in that way, they will thus prove to the francophone minorities, and even the Francophone majority in Quebec, that the whole country accepts the principle of the equality of both official languages, and that attitude should dissipate expectations of separation.
In this vital area, how to combat the forces of assimilation which threaten the survival of Francophones outside Quebec, co-operation between the federal and provincial governments is desirable. I shall, therefore, also be consulting with the provincial governments over the next few weeks on how we may best respond to the needs of these endangered communities.
When we speak of official language minorities, there is a tendency for some to think only of the Francophone communities living outside Quebec. But we must also remember that in Quebec there is another official language minority, the English-speaking population of 800,000. This minority, historically strongly established, now feels threatened. As a result of the present policies and future objectives of the present Quebec

government, the Anglophone community feels undermined and insecure. Many of its members feel that the objective of the present provincial government is to force them out of their province into other parts of Canada. The federal government, just as it is concerned with the threat of assimilation of Francophones outside Quebec, is concerned over the sense of insecurity presently felt by Anglophones inside Quebec.
I have recently received approaches from the community for help to document their concerns, especially with regard to the shifts in population as well as businesses, and to outline the economic effects of these changes. As with the Francophones outside Quebec and the help of a similar nature which we gave them some years ago, we feel disposed, in all fairness, to offer similar support to the Anglophones in Quebec if requested, so that they can better understand their future and make representations to the relevant authorities for their survival. We are prepared to support projects that encourage creative rapprochement between English and French-speaking Quebeckers, activities that assist English-speaking Quebeckers and their associations to become bilingual, and programs which enable English-speaking Quebeckers to preserve their cultural heritage.
In all the other provinces there are strong associations representing the Francophone minorities, but for a variety of historical circumstances such an association has not developed in Quebec. If it appears that English-speaking groups are now ready to co-operate with each other and develop the basis for an organization or structure of organizations representing them as an official language minority in Quebec, we would be prepared to encourage and support this development. I believe such a structure could be a positive intermediary between the English-speakers in Quebec and the provincial government, as well as a valid spokesman vis-a-vis the federal government. [Translation]
To give concrete proof of its interest in Francophones outside Quebec, and Anglophones within Quebec, the government has decided to increase considerably the credits earmarked for the official languages minority groups program. We intend to set aside for this program an amount of $75 million in the next five years. Thus, we will be better able to meet the needs of official language minority groups in the various parts of Canada.

My remarks this afternoon have focused on the language policy. I do not have time to describe at length the problems and opportunities we face in cultural policy, although this is an area of my department's responsibilities about which I have intense concern.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to take part in the debate on the address in reply to the Speech from the Throne. I wish to begin with a few words on multiculturalism in Canada. 1 am not sure whether the intentions of the government in 1971 were serious when the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) announced such a policy. 1 do not know whether that policy was introduced by the government for the purpose of political expediency, to woo the ethnic voters in Canada who comprise more than 30 per cent of our population.
I do not know whether it was an honest attempt to involve Canadians whose origin is other than that of the two founding nations, English and French, to bring them more into the mainstream of Canadian life and no longer regard them as second-class citizens. Whatever the motives of the government, 1 can assure them that with their introduction of a multicultural policy in Canada they now have a tiger by the tail and dare not let go.
Despite all the vehement protestations to the contrary by various spokesmen on multiculturalism on the government side, the objections of certain Quebec caucus members to multiculturalism have been so great that there is no doubt in my mind that the Prime Minister and the cabinet would have terminated this policy once and for all had there been any let-up in the flak produced by this side of the House and the protestations from many of the 71 or so ethnic groups against such a move.

October 27, 1977
The Address-Mr. Mitges
Mr. Speaker, I like to look upon myself as an optimist as far as as multiculturalism in Canada is concerned. We now have a minister who I think is interested in the subject and sincere in his idea for the further progress of multiculturalism in Canada. This is not to detract from the three former ministers; 1 am sure they did their level best, under very trying circumstances and in the face of much cabinet opposition, to push forward programs designed to further multiculturalism. The new minister has come out vigorously in support of qualified persons of ethnic origin occupying more positions of high responsibility in government and in Crown corporations, the greater involvement of "ethnics" in the broadcasting field and other areas.
The minister may be filled with good intentions, and there is certainly nothing wrong with having good intentions. But it remains to be seen whether those good intentions will lead to action and firm direction, and how much influence the minister has with his cabinet colleagues. As the critic for multiculturalism on behalf of my party, 1 am willing to give the minister a little more rope, a little more time in which to familiarize himself with his new portfolio before I cross-examine him for the good of multiculturalism across Canada.
I should like to say a few words about our country. I shall speak very bluntly. It is necessary to be blunt, not because there is any particular virtue in inflaming passions, arousing resentment or making people uncomfortable, but because this country will only recover from its national despondency if we are all prepared to tell it as it is and, further, to persuade all our people that the country is worth saving. This means facing reality and understanding it, and having the moral courage to insist on the best that is in Canadians because the times demand the best.
There were, and still are, people who say the idea of Canada is illogical, that it cannot work, that assimilation by the United States is inevitable, that our country defies the laws of trade, and that it is impossible to contain in one country many different linguistic and cultural groups. Such arguments have been with us since the beginning. They are being resurrected again, not only in Quebec but in other parts of Canada. But the reality defies those arguments because, on the whole, since confederation we have been remarkably successful. We have built a great country under circumstances, at times, of immense difficulty. Moreover, this has been done within the framework of three parliamentary institutions and a high degree of civility under the rule of law. We have not been perfect, and given the nature of mankind we are unlikely ever to be perfect. But we most certainly have not been a failure. This is the first reality and it is the starting point for any debate on where we go from here.
The second reality is that the complaints raised with regard to our country have all been voiced before. Quebec separatism, or independence as Premier Levesque chooses to call it, is not new. A deep and constant sense of nationalism has always been part of the French-Canadian presence and in its extreme form has never been far from the idea of separation. Western alienation is not new. Atlantic Canada's grievances did not

begin yesterday. Because of the vast geographic size of Canada, its diverse economic opportunities and the linguistic and cultural differences which characterize it, there have been, and probably always will be, strains within confederation. That is no reason for wringing our hands and giving up. What it means is that we must resolve these problems, perhaps not to the satisfaction of every dissident in the country, because that is impossible, but to the satisfaction of the large majority of our people. It means we cannot take things for granted. It means that the dynamics of our society imply constant change, and that the task of government and citizenship is to face up to reality and find solutions.
Those of us whose heritage is neither British nor French realize that our cultural aspirations may well be severely limited during the next few years as the federal government and provincial governments continue their negotiations on the political integrity of Canada. We may well be asked to compromise certain of our multicultural ideals for the sake of accommodating the linguistic demands of the present Quebec government. The disturbing fact is that the government of Quebec is determined to protect the culture and linguistic rights of the French-speaking population of that province, while showing little concern for the rights of other minority groups, including those of French-Canadians outside Quebec. I should like to take a little time in which to review and examine the assumptions behind Canada's policy of multiculturalism in order to place my remarks into context.
There were several sound reasons for the development of a multicultural policy. Those reasons are as valid today as they were six years ago when the policy was first enunciated. Let us consider two of the assumptions behind that policy. First, the degree of cultural diversity which exists in Canada rules out the melting pot approach to national unity. It has been argued that cultural diversity has been of positive benefit to the development of Canadian society. There are few people who can look back over the last 20 years-to the Bill of Rights, to the centennial year and EXPO, to the Olympic Games and, more recently, to the establishment of a Human Rights Commission-and fail to realize to what extent these events have drawn upon the strength of a country whose culture rests upon the full and equal participation of all its ethnic groups. The events of the past year have not lessened the reality that Canada's vitality depends to a large extent on its cultural diversity. Indeed, many would claim that this is the example which Canada sets for the rest of the world.
In the second place, the cultural diversity of this country is a significant bulwark of our democratic principles. Tolerance of cultural diversity in a nation is one of the best measures of the strength of its democratic institutions. Conversely, when democracy is on the wane, minority groups are often the first to suffer. In this respect, I think any multiculturalism policy must establish very high standards of racial, religious and ethnic understanding for us all. I do not believe we are prepared, as a nation committed to democratic freedoms, to accept anything less.
October 27, 1977

We should now proceed to examine the role of the recently elected Quebec government in the context of our concern for the preservation of the cultural diversity of Canada and the security of our democratic traditions. Undoubtedly, there is a great deal of sympathy among Canada's ethnic minorities for the aspirations of Quebec's Francophone population-probably more than Rene Levesque is aware of. In particular, roots which have their origin in territories under Soviet occupation must possess an excellent understanding of the concern of French-Canadians for cultural survival.
Sympathy and understanding should not, however, stop us from being critical of the activities of the Parti Quebecois when it threatens our vision of a Canadian nation based on tolerance and encouragement of many different cultures, especially since that vision should not, and does not, conflict with the special rights of French-Canadians.
Two recent examples of the Levesque government's reaction to multiculturalism are its stand on native language rights and the imposition of bill 101. Both these situations leave much to be desired in terms of tolerance and respect for minority rights. The government's reaction to the James Bay natives demands that English continue to be their second language, a matter which is guaranteed by law, has the appearance of being very high-handed and something of an overreaction, to say the least. The situation respecting the educational freedoms of other minority groups further demonstrates that the Levesque government holds less than a sincere desire for a new and separate multicultural state which it continuously expounds.
On the basis of this kind of evidence, I believe Quebeckers have the responsibility to pay very close attention to the intentions of their government. The integrity of the Levesque government will depend, as far as the multicultural community is concerned, on the implementation of policies which match the democratic freedoms and cultural tolerance of our over-all Canadian society. There is no doubt that the Parti Quebecois has introduced an element of uncertainty with regard to Quebec's future, to say the least. Whatever the troubling aspects of the Quebec election, there is, in one sense, a possible benefit from it for the entire country. I think the election has started Canadians thinking seriously about what Canada means to them and what each of them would lose in both a material and an emotional sense if this country ever broke apart.
Those of us of non-British and non-French origin stand to lose if Quebec should leave confederation. In so doing, we must face certain realities, the first of which is that Canada might well not be a multicultural country if not for the French-Canadian presence. It is an accepted fact that the French-Canadian determination to preserve their language and culture provided the basis for other groups to make similar demands. The best evidence of this can be found in the proceedings of the bilingualism and biculturalism commission. It was not until a royal commission was set up to study the
The Address-Mr. Richardson
bicultural nature of Canada that members of Canada's other ethnic groups found the opportunity to demand official recognition of the multi-ethnic or multicultural character of Canadian society. However, just as the French-Canadians set an example by their struggle for cultural survival, they would also set an example by their secession. The fear that Canada's cultural diversity could contribute to the country's fragmentation would suddenly become a reality.
Ironically, however, French-Canadians have also provided some of the strongest opposition to multiculturalism. This opposition has stemmed largely from a fear that multiculturalism was oriented toward placing French-Canadians on the same level as other ethnic groups, and that this situation would lead to their slow but inevitable assimilation into the Anglophone community. This opposition to multiculturalism on the part of French-Canadians is the second reality that we must face. Thus, if we have concern for preserving Canada as a united and multicultural nation, we must accept certain obligations. Above all, we must counter the separatist argument that the Canadian kind of community is not worth preserving. The separatists offer different reasons for their position-some cultural and some economic. To all but the most romantic separatists, we can demonstrate that it makes better economic sense to change arrangements within the country than to set up a separate shop.
There is no question that we live in a world of mass production where economic security depends upon the production of large volumes of goods and, as well, access to large markets. In the modern world, as the Belgians, the British, the French, the Germans and others have found, the way to make more money and to keep more money is in having larger trading units, not smaller ones. One of the most effective weapons against the separatist inclination in Quebec, in the west or wherever else it might arise, would be a coherent national economic policy to stimulate steady economic growth, and to provide real job opportunities for all Canadians. But an equally compelling case is cultural. The culture we value, whether it is Quebecois, or Ukrainian-Canadian, Greek-Canadian or Albertan, can only thrive in a broad community like Canada whose tradition is to respect differences.
Multiculturalism works toward heightening the awareness of Canadians to the importance of cultural diversity. It sensitizes Canadians to the important connection between languages and culture. It refutes the argument that the minority must conform to the will of the majority on all issues. Any step in the direction of a more just and a more democratic society can only serve to benefit not only French-Canadians but all Canadians.
In conclusion, let us remember that only by recognizing the legitimate aspirations of others can we ensure the recognition of our own.

Mr. Speaker, the Speech from the Throne read to us by the Queen calls on Canadians to rediscover the spirit of unity. My purpose in entering this debate is to make what contribution I can to the achievement of that all-important goal. I fully agree with the

October 27, 1977
The Address-Mr. Richardson
hon. member for Louis-Hebert (Mr. Dawson) when he said that national unity was the main subject contained in the Speech from the Throne. I should like to express my appreciation to him and to the hon. member for Malpeque (Mr. Wood) for the thoughtful and confident way in which they opened the debate. I might also include a word of congratulation to the hon. member for Grey-Simcoe (Mr. Mitges) who preceded me and also, if I may, to one of his colleagues, a fellow Manitoban, the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Epp), for the outstanding contribution which he made to the debate earlier.

1 want to talk about national unity as I see it and as I understand it. As a member of this House for almost ten years, I say to colleagues on both sides that no one wishes to see a united Canada more than I; and no one wishes to have Quebec and Quebecers as a part of Canada more than I. 1 want to say with equal conviction and, I hope, Mr. Speaker, with equal clarity, that I believe the government has been trying to achieve unity in the wrong way. I believe the government has been leading us in the wrong direction. The evidence for what I am saying is everywhere. We are not achieving unity; the country is more divided than ever.
In these circumstances, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the government have no choice but to ask themselves whether the policies that they have been advocating are in fact unifying, or have their policies contributed to the serious division that now exists in Canada? I believe there is an answer to Canadian unity, Mr. Speaker. I believe it is not too late for Canadians as one people to achieve true unity. But before we can state the answer clearly, we must find out what went wrong.
I should like to speak about four fundamental reasons why Canada is now a deeply divided country, four examples of the way Canadians have been led in the wrong direction. First of all, as many other members have done, we must look at our history. For the first 100 years we were on the right track. We were working together. We were building the grand design set out by the Fathers of Confederation. From confederation to Expo we showed every evidence of becoming the model nation of the world. We increased our productivity. We increased our population. We fought and helped to win two world wars in the cause of freedom. In this and in other ways we continuously increased the respect in which Canadians were held by other peoples around the world. At the end of our first hundred years Canada was standing on the threshold of greatness. What went wrong? I believe the verdict of history will show that the decade of the sixties was the decade of division. In the 1960s Canadians were taken off the track.
If we are to identify one day, one point in time and place where Canada took the wrong turn, that day would be July 19, 1963. It was on that day the government established the terms of reference of the Bilingual and Bicultural Commission.

speechtext: From that time on, instead of talking about all that unites us, led by the government, Canadians talked increasingly about what divides us. subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY

Instead of talking about unity, the government talked about the duality of the Canadian personality. Since the mid-sixties, since the fatal turning point in 1963, we have increasingly been negotiating with each other, not so much as Canadians but as two separate and competing peoples, and we have been led to believe that the granting of concessions is somehow the road to unity. This is our second fundamental mistake.
I should like to say as clearly as I can that if the granting of concessions to Quebec, whether in the form of increased power for the government of Quebec or in the form of increased language rights, could achieve unity I would be the first to be calling for more concessions. But all the evidence and all our experience to date shows that instead of creating unity, the result of concessions of this kind is to increase disunity. The net effect is to strengthen Quebec nationalism, instead of strengthening Canadian nationalism. This paradox, that concessions that are intended to achieve unity actually result in disunity, has been set out clearly and explained in recent articles by Canada's most eminent historian, Donald Creighton.
A third cause for the deepening division within Canada is the conviction of the Prime Minister about the advantages of national bilingualism. Nowhere is the Prime Minister's misunderstanding of the reality of Canada more apparent than in his speech to the House last week. As reported on page 38 of Hansard for October 19, just after he talked about equality for the French and English languages the Prime Minister made these remarkable and revealing statements: "We are made for bilingualism", and "bilingualism is the very condition of our existence".
I listened to him say these words in the House and wondered how it was possible for anyone to so seriously misread and misunderstand the reality of Canada. Through you, Mr. Speaker, I ask the Prime Minister to ponder his own words. Through you, I wish to tell the Prime Minister that millions of Canadians do not feel they are made for bilingualism.
October 27, 1977

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Millions do.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Millions of Canadians who fully respect the use of the French language in Quebec and who want to accommodate Quebec's aspirations within a stronger Canada do not believe that bilingualism is the very condition of their existence. Do the people of Halifax or Edmonton believe that they are made for bilingualism? Do the people of St. John's, Newfoundland or Vancouver, British Columbia, really believe that bilingualism is the very condition of their existence? If that is how the Prime Minister sees Canada, it is easy to understand why this country is so divided.
Another part of the Prime Minister's speech last week revealed the potentially most serious and dangerous cause of division in Canada, and that was in his reference to the constitution. If we read carefully the Prime Minister's words as set out on page 38 of Hansard of October 19, it is clear that he wants his words and his wishes, his kind of Canada, to be locked into the constitution. It is clear that the Prime Minister would like his vision of Canada to be placed above parliament and beyond the reach of parliament, now and in the future. He talks about arrangements to guarantee in the constitution that the French fact will be inalienable in Quebec by any government, any administration, any federal parliament.
To make his position clearer, he goes on to say that rights should be written into our constitution so that they become definitely inalienable and cannot be abolished through a whim or arbitrary decision by any government. Mr. Speaker, who is being arbitrary? When did the will of parliament become a whim? The Prime Minister knows that legislation passed through parliament by his majority can be amended or changed by parliamentarians in the future. He is not prepared to leave the judgment to future parliaments. He wants to entrench his vision of Canada, his concept of appropriate language rights, in the constitution. He seems determined to place these rights beyond the reach of parliament, beyond the democratic process.
The proposal he is now trying to sell to the provincial premiers is that language rights be entrenched in the Canadian constitution and that the constitution cannot be changed in the future without the approval of the province of Quebec. Of all the changes to the constitution being proposed by the Prime Minister, this House should be most concerned about the procedure being recommended to amend the constitution. This concept of a "single province" veto over changes in the constitution of Canada is undemocratic and unacceptable.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
It is the majority of Canadians, not one province, who must have the right to approve or to disapprove changes in the constitution of Canada. Perhaps now that the Prime Minister has shown some interest in holding referen-dums, he will take up a suggestion I made more than a year ago and give consideration to the proposal that important changes in the constitution be made only with the approval of a national referendum. In this way the majority of Canadians
The Address-Mr. Richardson
could determine the kind of Canada they would like to have in the future.
My message has always been that it would be wise for Canada to keep our serious language difference at the level of statutory law, which is amendable, and not at the level of constitutional law, which is not amendable except by a rigid amending formula. Canada's Official Languages Act is amendable. In fact, the Speech from the Throne calls for amendments to the act, regardless of what those amendments are. None of us in this House should forget that it is the ability to amend statutory law that gives Canada the flexibility to grow and to change and which confirms the supremacy of parliament.
Surely this is not the time to try to make our differences permanent. I warn the House and I warn the Canadian people that if we entrench the concept of duality in our constitution, if we lock our difference into our fundamental law under a Quebec veto, we will have become two nations and we will have divided Canada forever. The Prime Minister and some others would like Canadians to believe that there are only two options: the separation of Quebec, or a bilingual Canada. This is not the case. By far the best option is to build in the future on the foundation set out by the Fathers of Confederation. It is not necessary to destroy Canada or to change Canada fundamentally in order to build the great Canada in which most of us believe. The Fathers of Confederation did not talk about two founding peoples. They did not talk about two equal national languages. They did not try to write into the constitution an amending procedure that would give a single province veto over future constitutional change.
Here in this House and across Canada, the only way we can be of use to each other is to be honest with each other. If truth is to be found anywhere, I have always believed it should be here on the floor of the House of Commons. It is in that spirit, Mr. Speaker, that I now want to state what I believe to be the answer for Canada. There is an answer that reflects the reality of Canada, a natural, common sense answer. The true answer is that there is only one Canada and Canadians are one people. The answer is to rediscover the spirit of one Canada which we have known in the past and which we can know again.
To do this we must learn that the true spirit of unity is not divisible. Unity can never be found by emphasizing duality and by accentuating diversity. To be one people we must increasingly find ways to be united by language instead of being divided by language. I believe we can do this and at the same time preserve the French language and culture. The answer is for two groups of Canadians to become increasingly bilingual. More English-speaking Canadians in Quebec should be learning French, and more French-speaking Canadians should be learning English. Fortunately, there are strong economic advantages, as well as cultural advantages, to be gained by both of these groups in learning, in each case, the majority language. It is obvious that English-speaking Canadians in

October 27, 1977
The Address-Mr. Hnatyshyn
Quebec are able to work more effectively when they are able to speak the majority language of Quebec.
It is equally obvious that opportunities for Quebecers are multiplied many times when they are able to live and work in the majority language of Canada and in the majority language of North America. It seems reasonable to believe that Englishspeaking Canadians who live in Quebec should want to learn the language of their province, and it is equally reasonable to expect that French-speaking Canadians should want to learn the language of their country. My heart tells me, and fortunately all the surveys confirm it, that the majority of Quebecers want to share in all of Canada and I know the overwhelming majority of Canadians want Quebecers to share equally in all of Canada. Once the reality of one Canada is understood and accepted, Canadians will be united as never before in our history.
The only workable, common sense goal for our country is an increasingly bilingual Quebec in a common language Canada.
