speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to enter this debate on the address in reply to the Speech from the Throne, and I join others who have extended congratulations to the mover and to the seconder of the motion, the hon. member for Louis-Hebert (Mr. Dawson), who is in the chamber this afternoon, and the hon. member for Malpeque (Mr. Wood).
We have heard a very interesting speech by the hon. member for Winnipeg South (Mr. Richardson) a few moments ago on the issue of national unity as he sees it. I was interested in his remarks, spoken, as they were, with the greatest sincerity and with great attention to delivery. I recall that the hon. member for Winnipeg South is one of those who joined a number of members who have left the cabinet for reasons of their own. At the time that he left the cabinet he indicated that he was not in a position to give unlimited support to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) on the issue of national unity.
I also recall another very telling fact, I think. If I am not quoting him out of context, I believe he pointed out that in his estimation, having served in the cabinet for a considerable length of time, this administration did not have the interests of western Canada at heart and was not serving western Canadians in the way it should.
Like the hon. member for Winnipeg South, I also want to make some observations on the important issues before our country, and on this administration. I have had the opportunity to observe this government since my election to the House of Commons in 1974 and it is from that perspective that I want to address my remarks today. I came to the House in 1974 with certain ideas about the role which western Canadians in particular should play in the House of Commons, and the role we should all play with respect to the question of national unity. My concern at that time, which continues today, is for the future of our country.

I want to say at the outset that some of the statistics and facts which I may quote have given me cause for great concern, a concern which is probably felt by the majority of members of the House. The fact of the matter is-and the hon. member for Winnipeg South alluded to it in his remarks-that the Prime Minister and his administration have given their whole attention and priority, almost to the exclusion of everything else, to the so-called issue of national unity. There is not one of us in the House who would not support in general the "motherhood" concept of continuing as one country on terms that are most acceptable to the majority of Canadians, terms that are flexible enough to accommodate all people and all provinces in Canada. But what has concerned me more than anything is that, in light of our very serious economic situation today, it does no good for ministers to suggest that we in this country are better off than people are in Bangladesh, and that we have a better standard of living here. That is not what we are here for. We are here to look at the situation in Canada and try to accomplish this country's potential on the basis of the resources and the people in it. We are not here to compare ourselves with the lowest common denominator in the world, whatever that may be.
While we have these serious problems-and I hope to document and underline some of them-the Prime Minister continues to play a game of politics with the the national unity issue. I suggest that is irresponsible, and it will also be dangerous to the continuation of Canada as one country in the future if the Prime Minster is elected for another term. When this debate was focused on the problems of our economy, the Prime Minister attempted again, in a way only he is capable of doing, to divert and deflect the debate away from the serious economic problems we have, to the question of national unity, by dropping the suggestion that he was considering holding a referendum. I thought it was a possible deja vu for all of us. On the question of plebiscites and referenda, the Prime Minister was almost saying, as my colleague the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) said in her remarks, that we in Canada are faced with the proposition of a referendum if necessary, but not necessarily a referendum. It harks back to the old conscription controversy during the Second World War.
As head of this administration, the Prime Minister has given us a legacy, with respect to national unity and with respect to the economy of our country, in which we cannot take very much pride. I do not want to look back to ancient history, but I wish to point out some facts from the days when this parliament commenced in 1974 and compare with them some of the statistics and facts we are faced with today.
In June of 1974, 469,000 Canadians were unemployed. Today, that number is 886,000. In 1974, in my province of Saskatchewan, 9,000 people were out of work. Today, there are twice as many, approximately 18,000 persons out of work, and this in a province which has had one of the lowest inflation factors in the country. Since 1974, prices have risen in the vicinity of 30.4 per cent. When we talk about the success of
October 27, 1977

the anti-inflation program in holding down inflation, I am not sure that figure gives much comfort at all to the people of the country generally.
Less than one year ago, our dollar-which is a reflection of the confidence of the people around the world in Canada-was worth $1.04 in United States money. Since then it has slipped to a low of 89 cents, and there is no indication that it will stop there, and no reaction on the part of the government except that it wants the dollar to float to what the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Buchanan), I believe it was, said would be a realistic rate of exchange in relation to the American dollar. In 1974, we had a $673 million government spending deficit. Now we have in the vicinity of a $9.2 billion deficit-almost one-twentieth of all the wealth we produce.
On the basis of these statistics and on the basis of the performance of the government in the last three years, if this administration is allowed to carry on for another three years the consequences will be catastrophic. In 1973, we had a balance of payments surplus. Now we have a $5 billion balance of payments deficit. In 1974, we exported crude oil. Now we import something like 365,000 barrels a day. In 1974, we had a relatively united country, compared with the situation today. Only last year the Prime Minister said that separatism was dead. Now we have Rene Levesque. In 1974, our real living standard rose by 4 per cent. Next year, in the final gasp of controls, workers will actually have their living standard reduced by about 2 per cent.
Those are the facts and the statistics we face as we start off this session of parliament and look toward the legislative program and measures this government is bringing before us for consideration. If the Prime Minister is sincerely interested in maintaining his cry for national unity, he will give priority to the state of our economy, because I suggest that that aspect of our business in this House is certainly an important factor in maintaining unity.
A person in Quebec who is unemployed is just as unemployed as a person in Saskatchewan. He has just as real a feeling of resentment about the system as an unemployed person in Saskatchewan. He has the same feeling, in every respect, that he is not being served by his government. While the question of the French language is important, it is not the only consideration. The sooner the Prime Minister discovers that, the better off our country will be.
I want to refer to the situation which existed at the time 1 entered this House, and to what has transpired since. I want to look back to some of the things we were promised in 1974. There were a number of promises and undertakings by the Prime Minister and this government. In the 1974 election campaign, the government promised a future far different from the one it actually delivered. In the elections of 1968 and 1972, the government bribed the electors with their own money. The government made $3 billion worth of promises. The government was far from telling Canadians, "They have to be told they are soft", to quote the Prime Minister, and "When the dollar falls about 10 per cent in one year it is because the world is telling us we are living beyond our
The Address-Mr. Hnatyshyn
means". That is what the Prime Minister said last Sunday, October 23.
The Prime Minister also said that Canadians need discipline, "and if they don't discipline themselves, we will discipline them". By "discipline" the Prime Minister was apparently referring to the whole proposition of controls, or worse. The Prime Minister was presumably referring to the government's promise, made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) in his mini-budget, to limit increases in wages and salaries to 6 per cent in the last year of the program. As I mentioned before, this will result in a reduction of about 2 per cent in the living standard of a great many Canadians. Obviously, one had to read quite a lot between the lines of the 1974 election rhetoric to find this reality. Just before the Prime Minister came into this House in 1974, he said:
One thing about the freeze is clear. We can't freeze the prices on goods coming into Canada from other countries. They won't accept our freeze. So while your wages are frozen, those prices will be going up. Wage and price freezes have already been tried in the United States and Great Britain. It didn't work there. And they won't work here.
The hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Stanfield), then the leader of the opposition, did not talk about reducing workers' incomes. The answer of the Prime Minister in 1974, in continuing his tradition as a confrontationist, was that he was going to wrestle inflation to the ground. On the basis of the statistics and the facts I have given, when the Prime Minister makes a statement of government policy I wonder whether we are to believe what we are hearing and whether we are to accept any statement of the Prime Minister as government policy.
One thing that has impressed me about the Prime Minister is that if he says something categorically, the chances are he will do the opposite, and if he equivocates the chances are that he will in some way carry out the proposition he has placed before the House.
I am glad to see the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) in the House, because I want to remind him of some things that were said about transportation, particularly as it relates to western Canada. I recall when the minister told a public meeting that if the Liberal government were re-elected, not one railway branch line on the prairies would be abandoned as long as producers delivered to elevators on the line and the elevators continued to operate. It sounded something like an Indian treaty, Mr. Speaker-"as long as the grass is green and as long as the sky is blue". I ask the minister if he has changed his position from that time and whether this was a commitment on the part of the government, because we now find rail line abandonment taking place. Promises were made concerning agriculture, also, during the last election campaign.
Now 1 want to turn to something else that is of interest to me. In the field of energy, promises were made that have been kept in the same way as were those made about transportation. In the past few days there has been some discussion about nuclear policy and the allegations concerning an uranium cartel. I am concerned about this and the revelations which

October 27, 1977
The Address-Mr. Joyal
have occurred in the last year, because of the substantial deposits of uranium in my province of Saskatchewan. During my time in this House I have been concerned about lack of a coherent policy for nuclear or uranium export and import. This area has been concealed by a cloak of secrecy almost as if we were still fighting World War II and were dealing with atom bomb secrets.
As far as I can make out, policy decisions regarding uranium exports and nuclear energy are made with very little, if any, public consultation. As a result, people have no way of assessing whether Canada is adopting the correct position regarding nuclear policy. A great number of matters have given rise to the fear that wrong decisions have been made in this area and that the federal government has not fulfilled its responsibilities.
Uranium is the responsibility of the federal government, yet we find this government has taken the "hands off' approach and has left it to provincial governments to hold public hearings on the matter. In Ontario there is the Porter commission dealing with nuclear energy, and in Saskatchewan there is the Bayda commission dealing with uranium policy. A good part of the terms of reference of that commission are outside the jurisdiction of the province and are within federal jurisdiction.
The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) has called for a public inquiry by a standing committee of this House or some other agency to ensure that the national responsibility set out in law will be honoured. As yet there has been no response from the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie) or anyone on his behalf. The government has failed in this area of responsibility. On the basis of the things that have happened in this area with AECL, unless the government comes to terms with it we are not only failing in our moral responsibility to this country, but in the moral responsibility we have to the world.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the old saying would have it, history has whims but no habit. Speaking this afternoon after the hon. member for Winnipeg South (Mr. Richardson), I feel that this maxim is not entirely accurate. Some of my colleagues have recognized that the first paragraph of the throne speech took up again, one hundred years later, a statement made by Sir Wilfrid Laurier in 1877:
We are here, said Sir Wilfrid, under the government of the Queen, happy and free.
It was during the reign of Queen Victoria at the time when the sun never set on the empire and when, to reassert the wish of Canada for its independence in front of its neighbouring republic, the monarchy seemed the best rampart. A hundred years have elpased since. The English sovereign, as the Canadian head of state, despite the pompous rhetoric and commotion surrounding her travels, is only a symbol.
Yet, if in earlier times we have been able to display the crown and the sceptre to show ourselves different from our neighbours, we must recognize today, as our country is going through an identity crisis, that the throne no longer hold its

mystic virtues, at least for most French-speaking Canadians. Being the well advised person she is, Queen Elizabeth was quite aware of this, for she stated during her Quebec visit in 1964:
A dynamic state should not be afraid of re-examining its political philosophy.
The soul, the character of a people is expressed through symbols. "Any culture", wrote Andre Malraux in Le Musee Imaginaire, "is the incarnation of a legendary soul; but no culture is based only on legends, and if ours is more than fairy tales for grown-ups, it is because for us the story of Antigone is that of brothers who were enemies ... Antigone was a young woman who, knowing that she may be buried alive, buries two princes who had died fighting-one for his country, the other against it-because they were her brothers..."
Sophocles' drama haunts our "national" conscience, so great is the risk of burying hope by staging a mortal combat pitting against one another two brothers whom history has changed into enemies.
Symbols are as essential to Canada's political culture, and thus to the knowledge of itself, as the imaginary and timelessness are to the arts of civilization. The legendary soul of a people does not express itself merely through its copper or stone monuments, figures that Beaudelaire calls "viable monsters", it continually feeds itself on the inexhaustible source of its symbols. Some authors, philosophers I must say, even maintain that the ills and crises of modern societies can indeed be explained by the absence of a myth particular to them. When Jung wrote one of his books Modern Man in Search of a Soul, he suggested that the modern world was in search of a new myth, which alone would enable it to find a new spiritual source and give it back its creative forces.
Pragmatists, and they are numerous in politics in the wake of Bentham, do not take exception to the obsolescence of the mythical language of Canada's political society. What is the use of symbols, they ask. This question, innocent in appearance, receives complex answers. Levi-Strauss, Barthes and Lefebvre have suggested difficult avenues. According to these authors, the symbol is exclusive: it should not be disputed in respect of its content, its sense, its meaning. The integrity of its qualities, they maintain, give it a power of gathering, of consensus. If it is contested, it loses its proper value, it cannot any longer be a mark of belonging.
By its very nature, said Levi-Strauss, a political society finds its own symbolic expression in institutions.
Mr. Speaker, in my opinion, symbolic efficiency is vital to the unity of the Canadian political society. Those who think that the symbolic language of our political culture is veracious, or that, in any case, the relevancy of the monarchy does not really matter, avoid part of the essential debates, that is to clarify the confusion which exists in the Canadian system between the function of Head of State of Canada and that of head of the government.
Anyone who claims to be honestly searching for a new sense to national unity will not forever be able to clarify that
October 27, 1977

ambiguousness. If we think that it is possible to build a politically mature country, we must ensure the relevancy of its symbolic vocabulary. Never will we succeed in unifying this country if its capacity for abstraction is cramped.
As long as the majority in the country forces upon the minority symbols which do not reflect its conception of the world, the Canadian society will go through growing pains which might not create a stir on the surface but will certainly prevent it from developing the same political culture-a body of references to an heritage which could be shared by two majorities.
In a study he published the year before the November 15 election, political scientist Leon Dion wrote, and I quote:
Rather, they concluded that to rule it was enough to provide bread and games-to alternate between the carrot and the stick-on the assumption that people, today as yesterday, are not very sophisticated in social and cultural matters. Here can we best see the importance the Parti Quebecois could have for French Canadians. The task that devolves upon that party is indeed far-reaching: will it be possible for that party to help giving at last a political expression to the culture peculiar to Quebecers as it is shown today by the "chansonniers", artists, labour unions, intellectuals, citizen groups and young people? This is ultimately the great, in fact the only challenge to be taken up by this party: independence and social democracy are only a political reduction of the real problem, a problem which concerns the "vouloir etre", the soul of the people.
The authors of the speech read last week would like to seek in the human mind the cause of the present state of dissatisfaction in the midst of plenty, concluding that this is also where the unity of the nation will have to take its roots. This thesis, taken from a Renan conference in the Sorbonne in 1882, leaves out one essential dimension:
Everything created by the mind, Giedion states, will have to be humanized, which means compensated by sensitiveness.
Too many Francophones, including a number of proponents of changes in the socio-cultural order, federal institutions have never been able to express completely the sensitiveness, the "vouloir etre" of the culture which is peculiar to French-speaking people. The great political debates which have agitated Canada have always left Francophones humiliated, wounded, offended in their "vouloir etre".
The majority of Canadians, in times of great decisions, used all their weight to break the differing will of its revolted minority. Though Francophones had to bow, in 1885, in 1917, in 1942 and again in June of last year before the fanaticism of the controllers and pilots, their right to differ, their will to resist have only grown stronger from it. And now I quote Karel Kocik:
From the political point of view, the vanquished is the one who allows the adversary to impose his views upon him, who judges his own actions through the eyes of his adversary.
If we are to rediscover a sense of unity, it will have to be through means entirely different from those taught us by the political history of Canada. Today, some would try to legitimize the political institutions established some 110 years ago by a national or local referendum. How demeaning for the lessons of history.
In October 1866, 21 Francophone members of parliament sent Lord Carnarvon, chief Secretary of State to His Majesty
The Address-Mr. Joyal
for the colonies, a petition requesting that the federal project be submitted to the approval of the population before receiving the royal sanction at Westminster. The petitioners, with judicious pen, wrote that if Confederation were accepted, and I quote:
... without the sanction of public opinion, and it is discovered at a later date that it is unacceptable to the majority of the people in some of the provinces, which (they believed) would certainly happen in Lower Canada, there will inevitably be violent unrest, either to have it recalled or to have it amended, which will lead to an era of trouble and dissatisfaction which will be highly detrimental to the interests of the various provinces and very awkward for the statesmen of the Empire.
This request was never granted, Mr. Speaker. The assembly disposed of the project of Confederation by a rather embarrassing vote; 26 French-speaking and 11 English-speaking members voted in favour, 22 French-speaking and three English-speaking members voted against. To submit to public approval a constitutional piece of legislation passed 110 years ago, after having rejected public consultation on the same issue, would be forgetting history. We must read over the speeches of the supporters of public consultation before Confederation came into being to realize that, long before us, members from Quebec had seen in the public will the basis of the political institutions of a nation.
It seems unacceptable to me that one should think of forcing a majority of Quebecers to stay within the present institutions because that is what the rest of the country wants. Nor could we reasonably want to have a constitutional framework approved today, when their representatives were denied public ratification 111 years ago. If this constitutional referendum that the federal government is considering is to have any meaning, it can only be after a new proposed constitution would have defined a new form of political society and provided French Canadians with new guarantees. Some will argue that all this is already in the legislation, the commitments, the statements of the federal government. It would be ignoring the reality to think that existing formulas are perfect and that we only have to adjust their implementation.
It is not enough to proclaim the equality of languages for this to become a fact in institutions and in practice. It is not enough to proclaim the equality of opportunities to make people forget that political dynamics is essentially a relation of strength in which the majority always wins when it wants to, unless the rules are rigorously modified, otherwise the objectives will be completely distorted.
A constitutional referendum is therefore simply a strategy to surprise or defeat adversaries. It comes first of all from the profound conviction that the participation of citizens in decisions which affect their future is a basic democratic value. Therefore, it should be determined if it is through a desire to apply this concept of democracy and include it in the constitutional amendment process that the federal government will introduce a referendum bill. Otherwise, it will be diverting for its own purposes a form of democratic institution whose contents and meaning are far above tricks and strategies.
When we go through democratic channels to decide the faith of states, we must ensure identical requirements and

October 27, 1977
The Address-Mr. Joyal
meanings for rights and freedoms. After the events of October 1970, members of the federal government denounced publicly the weaknesses of Canadian legislation, and the War Measures Act in particular, to meet such exceptional situations while respecting as much as possible civil and political rights and liberties. It is unfortunate that despite the commitment made by the government leader in the House on October 27, 1975, a bill designed for such situations has not yet been introduced and the government has made no mention of it in its inaugural message.
As soon as there is a conflict-
-wrote Julien Freund-
-man is immediately willing to take side with one of the opposing parties, precisely to give it a retributive value, even by distributing guilt unilaterally. Is this not an admission that we give strength to the value of a judgment when we recognize that the cause of one of the opponents or antagonists is good and just and that of the adversary is wrong and iniquitous?
The crisis with which we are now faced is too likely to give rise to bellicose manicheism for us not to recognize as urgent the need to restrict the power of the state. The commitment to serve rights and liberties can be measured first of all by the urgency with which we prevent and solve situations where they could be threatened. The elimination from our statutes of potential abuses of power is a necessity which must command all our attention in our present uncertain situation.
To exist as a country, can Canada have other institutions than those defined in the act of 1867? That is the question that many of our fellow citizens, including sincere men and women whose commitment to the defense of a more open and more just society has been proven, are asking themselves about the alternatives that have been identified as a "third option."
Those people are indignant because of past injustice, worried, perhaps in a Montaigne kind of way. People who do not want destruction or disruption, those frequently used words in politics, but try in sober thought and in respecting other people's opinions, to reach a consensus around values which might bring about a common will to live which is closer to everyone's aspirations. That approach, which is essential in the definition of the balance we are aiming at, lies in fact on two virtues: tolerance and idealism.
The first comes from what Mounier once called "la dramati-que d'autrui". The second comes from an understanding of freedom which says that "the theory where truth will arise is the attitude of a man who distrusts himself'.
That should reassure all those to which individual as well as national independence are not absolutes. To try and specify values which the act of 1867 did not foresee is a process which cannot find a solution in obsolete formulas.
Far from being the so-called wizards of constitutional alchemy who unwittingly fell into the semantic trap, the "damned of the third option" stand a far better chance of being the explorers of the rediscovery of the sense of unity than of being the heretics of the official orthodoxy.
The inaugural address dealt at length with the present economic conditions; if it suggests immediate steps to face the
(Mr. Joyal.)
setbacks of an ailing economy, it barely touched on the more exacting concerns of those who beyond the immediate feel as Pisar that "the economic and moral aspects of our future cannot be dissociated".
This awareness of the stakes conveyed by the trend of the economic growth is not ignored by some government members. Did the Minister of National Health and Welfare not state on November 3, 1975 that:
Few are aware, for example, that in 1973, the families included in the lower 20 per cent of the economic ladder received only some 6 per cent of the total income, while one Fifth of the people at the higher level got about 39 per cent. It has been extremely difficult to alter those ratios throughout the years, the gap being almost similar in Canada in 1951 as it is 25 years later.
This cool and clear-headed finding appeared a few weeks later in the Prime Minister's remarks at the end of the year:
We have not been capable of making good use of our free market system. What this system has eventually brought us is nothing but very high unemployment and inflation rates. We cannot go back and keep the same habits, the same behaviour, the same institutions.
There is no need to recall, Mr. Speaker, the outcry that these remarks generated mainly from banking and credit circles. The present structures simply cannot modify the power relation that has been established in this country between its various economic components. Although Canada sets aside more than 28 per cent of its budget for transfer payments, such operations have only helped at best in freezing the gap between incomes as it stood in 1951. They do not contain the seeds of a reduction of that gap. It seems that we have reached a certain ceiling in the capacity of the present programs to modify the scale of incomes. In a study released in March 1976 by a committee formed under the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs called "Dynamic change and accountability in a Canadian market economy", the elements of a new approach were formulated which opened avenues for a redefining of the role and the limit of government action within the framework of a free market economy.
The lack of reference to this subject in the Speech from the Throne leads us to believe that for the present, the government is more concerned about lowering the rates shown by statistics than about performing an exercise of deep reflection on the orientations, the choices and the inequalities brought along by our present economic structures.
Mr. Speaker, I will conclude my remarks by saying that our country is engaged in a period of deep and intense reflection. Simplifications, historical shortcuts and mystifications must not prevail and make us lose track of what has always inspired the century-old resistance of Francophones throughout the times-their refusal to become assimilated and be part of an homogeneous society.
They have historically asked for justice; they have always recognized their own minority rights which were broader than they ever were granted elsewhere in Canada. They have always thought that being just was a way of questioning freedom as practised by the various seats of power, be they of a governmental or business nature. They have come to a moment in their history when they will no longer plead or beg
October 27, 1977

for the right to be different, they just want to "live their difference".
This is the sole responsibility resting upon us: to review entirely our political society to make sure that the laws and institutions of the country are a guarantee and reflect, in their action and their operation, the difference which has always characterized us.

speechtext: Thank you. I noted with interest that the hon. member referred to a play by Sophocles, the play "Antigone", in which the central character was driven by what the critics call hubris to separate himself so much from society that finally he destroyed himself. I wonder why the hon. member did not elaborate on that aspect, rather than on one of the minor elements of that play.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Speaker, 1 will gladly remind my colleague on the other side of the House, that Antigone did not commit suicide, but was condemned to be buried alive and that she symbolized love in mythology, in classical drama. As she was being walled in Antigone said: "I was not born for hatred but for love". And both her brothers lost in action specifically represent the hope she entertained of symbolizing love when, accepting the verdict of the jury, she preserved the two forces which had led to her death-hatred and love.

I am delighted to take part in the discussion of the Speech from the Throne. It is a great honour to have such an opportunity after the recent opening of parliament by Her Majesty the Queen.
October 18, the day of the throne speech, was a day of very special meaning to me, because it marked the first anniversary of my election to parliament.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
So it was especially meaningful to me to hear the fine moving and seconding speeches of two members who also came into parliament as a result of by-elections. This first year has brought many insights and a new appreciation of the extent to which the spirit and decisions of this House reach out into our national life. I am proud to represent the people of Ottawa-Carleton. They have taught me, inspired me and shown me time and time again that it is not the great systems
The Address-Mrs. Pigott
or the great laws which make a nation, but the life of its people.
The one event of the royal visit which stood out for me was the mingling of people of all faiths and ages, some of them in wheel-chairs, at the interfaith service as they gathered beneath the beautiful Peace Tower to pray for Canada. I felt hopeful that morning.
1 do not wish to get into a debate at this time about the role of the monarchy in Canadian history, but I should like to mention one thing: during the royal visit, our attention was drawn to a woman who has performed her duty for 25 years in a most outstanding way as Queen of a Commonwealth embracing 36 nations and a quarter of the world's population. The superb record of Her Majesty the Queen is a great example to the government of this country which has repeatedly promised that the role of women is going to be more fully recognized, though I am afraid they have paid only lip service to that idea. Why could not the government have marked the visit of this outstanding woman by making a firm commitment to appoint a significant number of women to all boards and commissions, in appreciation of the role of women in Canada?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Cultural and linguistic equality are important, but sex equality is also important to this country.
I would like to speak for a few minutes about decentralization, Mr. Speaker. There are many upsetting aspects of the recently announced program of decentralization of government departments. Most disturbing to me is the fact that planned decentralization, which could well have been a positive step, has been replaced by a kind of manipulation and blatant political opportunism which has created what a local newspaper has called "The new Acadians."
Public servants recognize that many companies in private industry move their employees, and it is an accepted practice in the armed services. The method of decentralization, however, leaves much to be desired. So much of decentralization has placed planning second to political expediency that public servants, 1 am certain, feel like chessmen on a board-pawns in a game.
Would it not, Mr. Speaker, have been more humane to decentralize by establishing new government agencies away from Ottawa, as was done, for example, with Petro-Can, rather than moving existing operations? If we examine the decentralization being carried out as an investment in human and financial terms, little credit can be given to the "broker". There is, for example, little indication that local labour markets will be improved by jobs moved to the regions from Ottawa and staffed from the capital too. Duplicate staffing is inevitable in order to facilitate communication between Ottawa and the regions. Overhead costs will rise as new buildings are erected to replace existing government-owned space left empty in Ottawa. As my colleague, the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker), explained in his fine

October 27, 1977
The Address-Mrs. Pigott
speech the other day, it is silly to argue that decentralization will help unemployment when specialized agencies are moved to other parts of Canada.
The most critical weakness in decentralization planning is that it overlooks the fact that people are being moved, not just entries on an organizational chart, or desks and chairs. The government cannot claim to have the best interests of Canadians at heart when decentralization is being carried out without consultation, and when 13 or 15 units being moved are destined for areas important to Liberal election hopes. As one observer pointed out, if private industry attempted such a move, the government would step in to protect the workers on the grounds that it was not part of the original agreement when they were hired.
There has been no consultation. The Public Service Alliance of Canada has called for a committee comprising government representatives, departmental people and union officials to work together in planning decentralization. Lack of such consultation poses a serious threat to morale in the public service. The task force on decentralization is an internal inquiry. The cost of decentralization is unknown. No master plan is available. The government has argued that only 11 per cent of the United States public service is based in Washington-ignoring the fact that 80 per cent of the so-called decentralized units are within 40 miles of that capital city. In any case, is the U.S. example appropriate to the Canadian situation?
This lack of information is compounded by the fact that many employees affected by the moves learn of the decision through newscasts or a memorandum issued on the same day that the moves are announced. The number one employer in Canada gives little evidence that it comprehends or cares about the lives of its employees. Planning appears to be a game in which a roll of the dice determines how many people will move, and a spin of the political dial determines where.
I should like to speak for a moment about housing and urban affairs, for me a new area of concern. Mr. Disraeli said: "Man is not the creature of circumstances. Circumstances are the creatures of men." Housing in Canada is proof of Disraeli's words. Over two-thirds of Canadians live in urban areas. Housing and urban development are important issues in this country. Canadian housing policy must recognize the wide-ranging nature of the housing sector. Suitable shelter is a basic right of every Canadian. Housing is a consumer item; it is the major investment of most families, and it is a part of industry, providing jobs, income and tax revenue. The development of our urban areas is a critical part of the quality of life of Canadians.
One of the most significant aspects of the housing sector which faces those forming policy is its extreme regional nature. Local conditions accelerate fluctuations on the urban scene as economic and social factors change rapidly. The steadying hand of long-term objectives and meaningful consultation among all levels of government must guide short-term measures aimed at specific problems. The present ministry of

housing and urban affairs has grown in isolation, losing its flexibility and sacrificing consultation for expediency.
The recently announced home insulation program is a sad example of this situation. Since the fall of 1975, the Progressive Conservative party has urged that energy supply measures be matched by energy conservation measures. The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) made this point clearly during the special energy debate in August, 1977. The International Energy Agency has questioned the apparent gap between promises and performance on the part of the government in relation to energy conservation.
I think the insulation program came into being because there was an August or September election looming in the distance, but a look at the insulation program discloses that it is discriminatory in that larger, non-taxable grants are allotted to the two provinces which, curiously enough, have Liberal governments. The program is inadequate. The estimated cost of insulating an average home is $900, while the maximum grant is $350. The head office for this program has been placed in a province which is not taking part in the insulation program. The lack of adequate regulation in this program has been a windfall for "quick buck operators". Inept installation and outright opportunism could cost Canadians more than money. As my colleague, the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath), has said, many people are turning their homes into fire traps.
I should also like to mention an area of concern to me which is very much part of my responsibilities but, more than that, for me is the focus of great interest. I refer to the handicapped. In mentioning a revised social services act, the Speech from the Throne touched on an area which is of great concern to me-the future of the one in seven Canadians who are handicapped. We too easily assume that an arthritic person is lazy or that a deaf person is slow. It is convenient to be sympathetic and patient about the obvious disadvantages of the handicapped. We do not often consider that we have our own, less visible handicaps which they must tolerate.
The Canadian Council on Social Development has pointed out that much of present policy as it affects the handicapped is fragmented, badly co-ordinated and inadequate. In fact, we must recognize that disabled citizens are entitled to access to the same community services as other Canadians. Birth defects could be prevented, rather than cured, if budgets were revised. Medical rehabilitation is a hit and miss affair. Responsibilities are so scattered that integration of services to the disabled is impossible. Disability payments are often wasted on administration instead of services. We have made age a handicap. How much consideration has been given to some sort of phased retirement, short work week or part-time work for the elderly?
On June 11, 1977, redistribution became official and new electoral boundaries were established in Canada. Since the Chief Electoral Officer is charged, among other things, with issuing instructions to election officers, and since the Chief Electoral Officer is responsible to the President of the Privy Council, a great opportunity exists for the government to issue specific orders to local deputy returning officers in each of the
October 27, 1977

federal constituencies to ensure complete accessibility of polling stations to those Canadians who are handicapped, especially the 100,000 or so Canadians who are wheel-chair users. I urge the government to consider these measures not as a matter of charity but as a matter of right. Harry Kemp once said:
I pitied him in his blindness But can I boast, "I see"?
Perhaps there walks a spirit Close by, who pities me.
Just a word about the future. Events of the past year have turned the thoughts and concerns of Canadians toward the future of our country. Options of many kinds have been brought forward. Changes in attitudes, however, may be more important than constitutional changes. The strains on national unity reflect many other serious problems. The spirit of trust necessary to sustain and build a strong Canada will develop only when citizens from all parts of Canada are able to explore solutions to our problems together and in good faith. We should remember that we talk of our resources and still largely ignore the energy and management potential of the half of our population who are women. Government employees are expected to be public servants, but they have so small a role in the decision to decentralize that they might as well be slaves.
Our urban centres, the largest of which could be provinces in their own right, must develop while coping with a lack of guidance, co-ordination and consultation, from an Ottawa government which does not co-operate or consult with the provincial governments about their concerns. We talk of democracy and then effectively block the ballot box for one in seven of our voters.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Right on.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Our future will be assured when this government begins to listen to the voices of the people and replaces the kind of politics which respond only to election promises.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is indeed a privilege to participate in the throne speech debate, especially in the Silver Jubilee year of the reign of our sovereign, Queen Elizabeth II. We were honoured, and indeed grateful, to have had Her Majesty participate in the opening of the third session of the Thirtieth Parliament of Canada.
I should like to take this opportunity to congratulate the mover and the seconder of the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne.
As I make my speech today, I vividly recall my emotions of excitement and humility when I delivered my maiden speech in 1957, at which time the Queen opened the first session of the Twenty-Third Parliament of Canada. Today, 20 years later, as we begin this session under the glare of television lights and the scrutiny of several cameras, my feelings are no less intense.
The Address-Mr. Haidasz
I hope televising our deliberations in this chamber will help to make our work more efficient and, above all, give our people a chance to see parliament in action.
Also, I welcome this opportunity to say how proud and grateful I am to represent the people of Parkdale in the House of Commons. They reside in an attractive part of west end Toronto on the shore of Lake Ontario. Parkdale has an interesting history of tradition and change about which we will hear more as its residents prepare for the celebration of its centennial in 1979. Many of my constituents were born in this great country, but many are immigrants or first generation descendants of immigrants who have adopted Canada as their country and, with their fellow Canadians, are generously contributing their work and their talents to make Canada an even better place in which to live and raise their children.
Parkdale is a reflection of the Canadian multicultural mosaic. Its people have family ties in other parts of the world and, therefore, international developments interest them very much. Many of them are closely following the Belgrade review meeting of the Helsinki agreement and the final act of the conference on European co-operation and security to which Canada was a signatory nation, along with 34 others, on August 1, 1975, in Helsinki.
As in some other countries, we have organized a parliamentary Helsinki group, reading the reports from Belgrade and watching the actions of governments. We have a parliamentary observer group in Belgrade and a group in Canada keeping in touch with concerned Canadians. The Helsinki agreement review conference, without a thorough examination of respect for human rights would be a mockery of the solemn commitments of 1975 and an abdication of the responsibility of governments to their people. I am sure the Canadian government will not be dissuaded from pursuing its humanitarian concerns so nobly begun and carried out during the initial negotiations of this conference.
We are particularly happy to hear in the Speech from the Throne that the goal of enhancing the rights and freedoms of Canadians can also be pursued through commitment to the principle of open government. An example of that commitment was the enactment of the Human Rights Act, the recent appointment of the Human Rights Commission and the Privacy Commissioner. In the future promotion of open government, parliament will be asked to approve the establishment of the office of ombudsman to deal with complaints arising from federal administrative actions.
As a member of parliament during the past several years, 1 have been astounded by the number of complaints from my constituents. Unfortunately, it is difficult to help them, in view of the bureaucracy and lack of such an office as that of federal ombudsman. Many of us who have been advocating such an office welcome this announcement of our government and hope it will bring greater and swifter redress to those Canadians who have been wronged.
I truly believe that the present session of parliament is shaping up into the most important and the most crucial session in our parliamentary career. Canada and the world are

October 27, 1977
The Address-Mr. Haidasz
confronted with many serious problems. Our industrial civilization is very seriously challenged by the energy crisis, inflation and unemployment. Governments and their people must rally and mobilize their will and resources to fight this grave threat to our socioeconomic survival.
Along with other members of the House, I welcome the government's initiatives announced in the Speech from the Throne which are evidence of the federal government's determination to give political leadership, strong government and an unwavering confidence to Canadians who are impatiently awaiting our best efforts in these difficult times. Therefore, this is not the time for half measures or petty politics.
During this period of wage and price controls, which had to be adopted to fight galloping inflation, Canadians have co-operated to restrain their demands on the economy and have achieved some successes. As the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) reported to us in his mini-budget address last Thursday, many companies have learned to deal with the problems of rising prices. We welcome the minister's announcement of measures designed to achieve a sustained growth in our economy of between 5 per cent and 6 per cent in order to bring down the unemployment rate and that the expansion should be led by exports and business investment.
As well, the minister explained the operation of the three root causes of our economy's setback, namely, weakened exports, increased costs of production, and lack of confidence. Then he proposed a five-point program to stimulate the economy without increasing the danger of inflation, namely, a phase-out of controls beginning April 14, 1978, a personal income tax cut of up to $100 for low and middle income taxpayers; further job creation programs; an employment credit for job creation, and the maintenance of strict restraint on government expenditures.
Also, he appealed for the help of all Canadians because government cannot do everything itself. He appealed to the opposition members in parliament to stop politicking and to start swiftly enacting measures proposed in the last budget and in the mini-budget of last Thursday. Time is precious, and each hour lost delays the benefits to our people and increases costs in general.
In the long term we must try to get all sectors of our population to co-operate with the government in developing without further delay an economic and an industrial strategy. Many of us have been asking for this for a long time, and I hope we will not have to wait much longer. The battle to provide more jobs, increase growth and ensure a stable economy will not be won without firm action and definite planning, and especially without the consultation and co-operation of business, labour and, indeed, all levels of government.
The recent reports of the Science Council of Canada and of our Liberal caucus's industrial policy committee should be given serious attention by our government in planning future economic and industrial strategy. In particular, the Canadian manufacturing industry should be strengthened in the face of

lower tariffs which are now being negotiated in Geneva at the GATT meeting. Some economists are even advocating a "Buy Canada Act", and others are recommending a greater effort to buy goods made in Canada. At this time I would like to appeal to the ministers in charge of the large economic portfolios to do everything possible to help save the jobs of employers of Northern Telecom, Anaconda Brass, and INCO where we hear that mass lay-offs are impending.
In harnessing our major programs to the objectives of a national industrial policy, we should try to create tax revenues instead of giving subsidies, and to develop industrial competence instead of relying on research from abroad. But the tax environment is very important to all such linked industrial objectives as specialization, research and development, and the processing of raw materials. The tax regime must be set so as to reinforce other measures and be related to achieving competitiveness. I think, also, it is time to re-examine and reform our tax structure as it applies to primary resources and secondary manufacturing industries, and to encourage the initiative of our businessmen, with tax incentives, to build and invest in Canada. Unfortunately, we hear that too many of our business and financial institutions are investing in states such as Florida where the tax structure is more favourable to them. These businessmen and investors are asking for more stable tax policies which would give them time to make long-term plans.
I also agree with the government that a special, comprehensive small businesses act is urgently needed to serve the needs of the smaller owner-managed sector of our economy, and that at this time of high unemployment our manpower training programs should be upgraded and made more practical, such as, for example, that the unemployed on these retraining programs be trained on the job. I think this will go a long way toward successfully relocating the unemployed people of our country.
We are particularly happy to hear from the Minister of Finance that this year and next year the government will be spending over $1 billion on direct job creation, and also the announcement by the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) that a special fund of $5 million will be made available to train our unemployed youth. We should also implement the 14-point program announced by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro), together with the establishment of a national consultative forum and fair comparison bargaining in public and essential services, as they are important elements of an over-all industrial strategy.
Some philosophers state that we are what we think, and some nutritionists state that we are what we eat. I believe that both are right. I also believe in the adage attributed to Juvenal about a sound mind in a sound body. That is why I was happy to hear about the new national policies on food and amateur sport. We are awaiting with impatience the forthcoming policy on recreation and physical fitness which is an important part of the government's legislative program for this and the coming year.
We learned with satisfaction, in the throne speech, that the government is taking new initiatives in the development of a
October 27, 1977

comprehensive national food policy by calling a national food conference next February after having received submissions from major sectors in this field. Canada does need an up-to-date food strategy, and I hope that during that conference expert nutritionists will be present who will study the problem of nutrition in Canada and, above all, the effect of the many food additives that are being allowed in our food products at this time.
The world is facing a food crisis which may be even more serious than the energy crisis. World stocks of grain are at a very low level, and there is increasing evidence that the pressure on food resources will not lessen. As was stated yesterday by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan), Canada has a unique and immense potential to increase its food production, in spite of its severe climate. The Canadian labour force and investment community have the capacity to develop a gigantic food industry in this country, as some economists have stated, such as Dr. G. Korey and Professor K. Eckhard, who in a major paper presented not long ago stated that Canada has the potential to become a world food bank, not only by bolstering secondary industry and becoming a great food exporter, and thereby reducing our trade deficits.
As a physician, I cannot refrain from reiterating my appeal to the government to increase its vigilance over the many new chemicals and other products introduced into our work and home environments. These new chemicals are dangerously altering our environment and are exposing man to growing amounts of harmful pollutants. As a result, today we are faced with the great problem of environmental diseases, including cancer, caused by asbestos, vinylchloride and other substances. We are faced with other environmental diseases, including birth defects, mercury and arsenic poisoning, chronic respiratory diseases, deafness, and many others. However, the proposal of the Minister of Labour for the establishment of an industrial safety and health centre should help to identify occupational health hazards and recommend any changes that are necessary as well as the strict enforcement of regulations.
1 should like to propose, also, that the federal government enact laws and regulations regarding special toxic substances, making it the responsibility of manufacturers to prove that their products are safe before they are put on the market. Such measures would help prevent new toxic substances entering the environment and endangering our health and lives, as well as upsetting the delicate ecology of our earth. We Canadians have reached a crossroad in our national life. Redesigning national socioeconomic policies is fundamental to the achievement of national unity. The urgency of constitutional reform and an economic strategy is made more acute by the separatist challenge from the Parti Quebecois government elected last November 15. So we welcome the intiatives of the government and the leadership of the Prime Minister expressed in his statement, that he is profoundly dedicated to the spirit and achievement of unity. The work of the task force on Canadian unity should assist Canadians to participate more actively in the debate and make a greater contribution to the future shaping of our country.
The Address-Mr. Haidasz
We are looking forward to the measures relating to the constitution of Canada so that a new federalism will emerge and receive the support and devotion of Canadians everywhere. We welcome the historic "Statement on Language" approved at the meeting of provincial Premiers last August, and the proposal to entrench in the constitution language rights in education. At this time I want to join with those Canadians who abhor the abrogation of English language rights in Quebec's language bill 101, and appeal to the government to assist the minority of Quebec to fight for its language rights.
I am sure we all welcome the government's proposal to amend the Official Languages Act and to clarify the role of the courts in safeguarding the equality of status of the official languages within the jurisdiction of the government of Canada, and the government's commitment to ensure greater availability of education in both official languages. 1 am sure we all agree that the great majority of Canadians are dedicated to the strengthening of bonds between Canadians speaking our two official languages and those belonging to our many different cultural backgrounds.
