speechtext: The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Dawson for an address to Her Majesty the Queen in reply to her speech at the opening of the session.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I take great pleasure in being able to participate in this debate because it allows hon. members to digress from the tedious rigidity of normal debate and to elaborate on some of the problems which are of particular concern to us, our regions, our provinces and our constituencies.
This is a particularly critical time in our country's history. It seems that every conceivable challenge which must from time to time be met by governments in the free world has been thrown at us. We are divided from within, in terms of geography and cultural goals and objectives. We have lost the confidence of our friends abroad, who are expressing discontent to us in economic terms. We are forced to direct all our attention to issues of national unity and to making patchwork repairs to our national fibre. This leaves us little time to address ourselves to the massive problems of unemployment and inflation which have caused much anxiety and fear among our population.
Many of the problems we now face cannot be isolated because they are all interrelated, one being the cause of the other and one equally and potentially as dangerous and disruptive as the other. Up to a year ago the government was able to compare our situation with that of other free countries around the world. Economic difficulties were a global problem brought on by the energy crisis, shortages and over-supplies of essential commodities, and significant changes in the behavioural attitude of people in the free world.
However, no longer can we make an analogy with other nations. The problems to which this government must address itself immediately are now peculiar to our own situation only. It almost seems that the methods and procedures which have been developed under our constitution-or the constitution itself-are no longer sufficient and broad enough in scope to accommodate the necessary changes which need to be made in order to correct some of the most serious imbalances which have occurred in our system.
In one of the brighter phrases of his speech, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) gave us an indication that he, too, has considered constitutional reform and Senate reform, using other countries as models, to satisfy the needs and objectives of regions and provinces. The Prime Minister made comparisons with the constitutional model of West Germany, where the upper House is appointed by region, which gives the senators a real presence in the nation's capital, allows them to take a real part in the decision-making process and allows them the power an upper House should have with respect to matters which relate to regional concerns and regional differences. It is obvious to me that that kind of reform is essential for us in
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Ethier).]
Canada if we hope to keep our country together. We must decentralize, not just the bureaucracy but the decision-making process as well.
Premiers' conferences are not enough, although the Prime Minister would likely prefer that. This would give the Prime Minister an opportunity to play the House of Commons off against the Premiers, and vice versa, an exercise in which he has already developed impressive skills. These skills are particularly evident when we assess the Prime Minister's behaviour in the establishment of bipartite negotiations with labour and business. The Prime Minister does not believe in tripartite negotiations in which three partners sit at one table in one room. He believes in talking to one partner at a time, exposing the other partner as the villain and never accepting any blame himself.
The reforms made in our system must be more fundamental than those we have seen. In spite of all the technological achievements over the past 50 years, we have not been able to bring our country closer together. We are, and likely always will be, dislocated by geography and economic and social realities. There is no amount of legislation which can bridge the gaps which will divide us into a number of regions with peculiar problems, but with unique opportunities as well. Our regions have developed their own priorities and objectives, and I consider it not to be of the gravest consequence that one of the priorities of the Quebec region, for instance, should not be to insist on linguistic duality at the moment but, rather, to assure that the great culture which has always been inherent in the French culture and linguistic group is preserved and that it be allowed to catch up in the economic area as well.
Our compatriots in the province of Quebec are not the ones who need to continue to chase after an illusive cultural identity, as we in the rest of the country need to do. Our compatriots in Quebec have other objectives, and they should have the right to pursue those objectives in a confederation.
As a matter of fact, having regard to the reality of Prince George, the Peace River country and all of British Columbia I fail to detect any enthusiasm toward the other official language. In fact, I could cite numerous examples of discontent which has been expressed to me in connection with the obsession of the Prime Minister to bring the French fact beyond an irreversible position in this country. It has been a divisive tool the Prime Minister has used to keep our country together, and his objectives have not been met.
All of us who have command of another language can appreciate the tremendous asset such skills can be, and our whole society would be enriched by the acquisition of such skills, but of so many other things which the individual likes to decide for himself this is probably the most critical one.
Parents who trace their ancestry back to cultures which do not find their roots in either the French and English cultures would likely aspire for their children to be able to acquire the language their forefathers spoke. Once upon a time, hon. members will recall, the government actively encouraged new Canadians to preserve language and cultural values they brought with them to their new homeland. Multiculturalism
October 27, 1977

has become a rather seasonal thing-the seasons change and advance with the prospect of a new election.
Like their compatriots in the province of Quebec, my constituents are not so much concerned about the fact that they may have trouble communicating with their government in two languages as they are concerned about communicating with it at all. The concern for the biggest part of my constituency is not the lack of a French channel on television, but the absence of any kind of television at all. Come to think of it, there are major settlements along the Alaska Highway that have no radio reception, and the great proud public institution known as Canadian National Telecommunications has yet to figure out how to keep a telephone working along the 500 miles of the Alaska Highway, which is in my constituency. The telephone line, like the highway itself, was inherited from the United States in 1943 and little has been done to improve the service.
Now, Mr. Speaker, 1 am speaking about the same Alaska Highway which is about to become the main staging area for the construction of the Alcan pipeline. As 1 do every year, Mr. Speaker, 1 travelled the route this summer. Already, there is excitement and activity related to the pipeline. For one thing, the oil industry is busy drilling for and developing the reserves of natural gas located in northeastern British Columbia. I assume that the industry is gambling that the government will allow it to export some of its harvest to the United States under the exchange or swap arrangement everybody talks about so much. It would deliver the overage of natural gas in our country to the United States, and take it back once the Alaska pipeline is built. Nobody knows, of course, and the people who will eventually make a decision are not yet saying.
There are surveyors, prospectors, engineers and entrepreneurs, but none knows what they are doing. They are not even telling each other. Residents along the highway are convinced that they really do not know themselves. What residents do know is that those who are most affected by what is to take place will be the last to find out. We have become accustomed to that. The pipeline will be no different than any other of the massive projects which have been conceived, planned, and put in place by some faceless industrial and social engineer in one of the concrete jungles in the south.
The highway itself was built under a crisis situation as a defence project. To those who had to live and work on the highway it has been a crisis ever since. The Peace River dam, the B.C. Railway, the pipelines which are already in existence, all have been built without any consultation with local and regional governments and agencies, service organizations or the people.
All have caused unimaginable hardship to local residents who are faced with all the negative side effects such projects bring with them, particularly during construction. It is almost as if it were the responsibility of people living in the frontier areas of our country to assure for their contemporaries in the cities and concrete jungles all the comforts of modern life, without ever being eligible for some of them themselves.
The Address-Mr. Oberle
The resources which are harvested in the north sell for one third less 900 miles to the south. A gallon of gasoline costs $1.50 in some places along the highway. This includes a 17 cents road tax the government of British Columbia adds for good measure to the 10 cents federal tax. The fact that the British Columbia government does not spend a nickel on the road which is entirely under federal jurisdiction does not need to be considered. But then the federal government disclaims any jurisdiction as well, so it is probably all right for the province to charge road tax.
You will recall, Mr. Speaker, my assiduous attempts to get the former minister of Indian affairs and northern development to consider the broadening of the terms of reference of the Lysyk Commission to add northeastern British Columbia to the study of the Yukon. The minister announced that he has no jurisdiction for areas within the provinces. This confuses particularly the native people in the area who look only to the federal government as the guardian of their special rights. Special rights indeed!
How unfortunate, for with the least bit of foresight and co-ordination of planning, a project such as the Alcan pipeline could accommodate without additional cost the legitimate aspirations of the people in the area. Who else but they themselves know best how to approach such a project from the human standpoint at least-how to work in the harsh, often inhospitable climate-how to use nature's incredible might to aid, not hinder, man's progress-how to arrange things in a way by which the finished product will have some lasting benefit-how to transform the facilities which will be required to service the construction crews, to serve the communities in the north, and give them greater stability once the project is finished.
Let me give you an example of what will happen instead. Because there are no facilities it will be necessary for the pipeline planners and contractors to build their own. They will require a very sophisticated communications network. Every hour of down-time can mean millions of dollars. They will build airstrips, machine shops, roads, camps with elaborate recreational facilities, power stations, waterworks and other services, the likes of which have never been seen in the north. After all, it will be mostly workers from the south doing the job who are not prepared to forgo any part of their accustomed lifestyle.
Northerners will watch in awe. It will seem like a scene from a science fiction movie, but they will not be allowed to play. The toys will all be taken away or bulldozed over once the last scene is shot. Scientists and engineers will let their imagination run wild. The latest technology will put the dream in place; then it will all be gone. It will even all be paid for- added to the cost of the gas which will keep southerners comfortable. Then it will be gone-just as quick as it all came. It is too bad it could not all have been planned just a little differently.
The only thing we in the north have to be thankful for is that gone as well will be the gamblers, the pimps and the prostitutes, leaving behind only their ugly memory-the rem-
80025 -2 3 Vi

October 27, 1977
The Address-Mr. Oberle
nants of a bad dream-or would nightmare be a better description?
My constituents, residents along the Alaska highway, will go back to staring at a blank television screen and waiting for a week at a time to use the telephone to communicate with the outside world-driving through mud, potholes, and dust to go to the doctor or dentist-taking their lives into their hands to pick up the mail 30 miles away.
I also travelled to Alaska this past summer to look at another pipeline. This one is finished. The boom has come and gone but some things will never be the same again, of course, for the people who were touched by the intrustion of the Alyeska project. Even cities like Fairbanks, well established, having been born out of the first major discovery of northern resources, gold, will have serious difficulties overcoming the shock southern planners and social engineers have perpetrated on it. They built new cities as well. There is a place that looks like a moon landscape-large buildings, pump stations, power stations, at Prudhoe Bay. There was nothing there before- just ice and snow, and a sparse growth of moss that makes up the tundra and provides food for the caribou.
Here the planners really had a runaway. There are beautiful parks under glass, with even some live southern species of trees. But most of everything else is made from a byproduct of the oil harvest. There is even a new futuristic social order which not only discourages intimate social contact between male and female workers but actually prohibits husband and wife from living together in the new plastic society. Our guide told us that sex is a misdemeanor and any infraction results in immediate dismissal of both partners. One of the workers gave us his definition of the term misdemeanor. He said the more we miss it, the meaner we get.
About the only scene visible in the area which bore any semblance to reality was a small number of caribou who were going about their business seemingly undisturbed by all the nonsense going on around them.
Isn't it ironic, Mr. Speaker, that the part of nature about which we were most concerned will be the least affected when all is said and done. However, the incredible human sacrifices that have to be made to satisfy the modern time social engineers who build the projects are most significant.
Let me serve notice on those who are about to embark on phase two of the Prudhoe Bay energy development that my constituents will want to have something to say about the sacrifices they will have to make. I would, however, also like to make it clear that we in northern British Columbia welcome that type of development. Unlike most other observers who pass their judgment from York University, we have learned to appreciate the stabilizing effect such a project can have on small communities, struggling to afford some of the most basic amenities of modern life.
The tax base and influx of permanent jobs in connection with the operation and maintenance of the pipeline is a welcome feature. In most cases we found that pipelines even

offer some positive features in terms of the environment. The rights of way provide better access to other resources. Moose and deer like the growth on the right of way and can therefore be seen in abundance, but most of the prosperity inherent in such a project will accrue to all Canadians.
We hear that $4 billion will be spent on Canadian material and supplies, and thousands of manhours will help to ease the unemployment situation. Is it therefore not reasonable to insist that the negative side-effects will, as well, be shared throughout our country?
Over the past few days 1 have demanded from various ministries the establishment of a technical planning committee to plan for the part of the country which I represent. I have demanded the ministry get involved and study what has happened in other projects and safeguard against negative side-effects in those areas so that my constituents will have a rightful place in Canadian society, like all Canadians, and be able to make their contribution to our country.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to extend briefly but sincerely personal congratulations to the television crew members in the House and the production staff. As a member of the special House committee which was given the mandate to implement television broadcasting of the House of Commons, I want to say that I am extremely satisfied with the tremendously good job of the CBC and the technical personnel whom they have hired to carry it out.
As with any throne speech, we are dealing with generalities.
I am now well into my seventh year in this House. It is not exactly a track record. However, in the time that I have been here I have not listened to a throne speech so lacking in national direction. As well, the mini-budget repeated the same policies that the Liberal government has been attempting to implement since 1963.
Let us not forget that the Liberal party has been in power continuously since 1963. It is very easy for a member on this side to say it is time for a change. That is a worn out phrase. However, if you look at what the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) had to say last Thursday, you will see that his department is still bankrupt of new ideas, policies, fiscal and monetary, and directions.
We are still talking in terms of solutions to problems which have not worked. We are still having legislation introduced that will give corporations large tax breaks, exemptions, and deferrals.
I was in this House two or three years ago when the former minister of finance, the Hon. John Turner, introduced a budget which was designed to create jobs and lessen unemployment. That budget was to stimulate the economy by putting more investment money in the hands of corporations. Several months after his budget, the then minister of finance sent a questionnaire to many of the large corporations directly affected by his budgetary measures. The reply that came back was very clear. The tax breaks, tax deferrals, rapid write-offs, depletion allowances and so on, had not in fact contributed to an increase in new jobs or a decrease in unemployment.
October 27, 1977

However, last Thursday evening we got another dose of the same old medicine.
I am beginning to wonder how much longer the Canadian people, whether they are aligned to my party, the Liberal party or the Progressive Conservative party, particularly the million plus out of work, the underemployed and the youth who have been educated at great cost but cannot find jobs suited to their education, will continue to accept the same old medicine that has not cured the economic ills of this country for the past ten years, particularly the last three or four.
I sincerely hope the majority of Canadians will think intelligently about the economic issues facing this country. 1 suggest, with great sincerity, that this is tied in with the national unity debate, crisis or issue.
I wish to make a few references to the national unity situation. 1 am convinced that if the economy were buoyant and unemployment were low in the province of Quebec, the young people in that province, as well as the middle aged and the older, would not consider separatism such a dynamic force. Let there be no mistake about it. Even though perhaps 30, 35 or 40 per cent of Quebecers would like to separate, and perhaps even fewer, there is the feeling in the province of Quebec that somehow they have developed despite Confederation. There is a feeling they have been able to preserve and develop their language and their culture in a sea of 220 million English-speaking North Americans. This has resulted in a tremendous sense of pride in the manner in which they have maintained their identity.
In fact-and I am speaking of Francophone Quebecers- they are a nation in the French meaning of that word. 1 am not quarrelling with that attitude nor am 1 quarrelling with this insularity, because they have had to promote themselves in order to survive. But I am convinced the average Francophone Quebecer would feel much more at home in Canada if the party presently in power federally, and in particular the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), a Francophone himself, had understood, not only in a cold and academic way but from the heart, the real feelings of the province of Quebec.
Some may say the hon. member who is presently on his feet represents a riding in southwestern Ontario. That is so. But, Mr. Speaker, on my mother's side 1 come from five generations of English-speaking Quebecers and 1 can tell you that I am not proud of the way in which some of my ancestors treated French-speaking Quebecers in rural Quebec, specifically in the Eastern Townships.
My grandfather refused to learn to speak French. My mother attempted to speak French but left the province for the prairies and, when she did, she forgot the French language. 1 can recall on the 11th range, not far from South Durham, little French children of my age-I am going back, now, to the 1940's-running around in the summertime without shoes, half-clad and poverty-stricken, in contrast to the children of English-speaking farmers who were not rich but who were certainly much better off. There has always been antagonism
The Address-Mr. Blackburn
between such groups. Speaking in terms of Montreal, it was between those who sat in the front offices and the Francophone workers who were behind on the assembly lines or production lines. It was the same in the rural areas. Very often the poorest farms were owned by French-speaking Quebecers while the best land was owned by English-speaking Quebecers.
The question I am getting at is this: what has the present Prime Minister done in the past ten years to try to explain the growing bitterness in Quebec, first apparent in the quiet revolution of the early 'sixties in the "maitres chez nous" period and reaching a dramatic conclusion on November 15 with the election of Rene Levesque and the Parti Quebecois, which was really a ceremonial seal being placed upon what had already occurred? If we are to understand the aspirations and determination of Quebecers we must bear these things in mind.
Let there be no mistake about it, Quebec is potentially a very rich geographic entity. It could trade with France and the French-speaking community overseas. It could "go it alone" although there might be years of trial and difficulty. Let us not forget that if they are determined enough to go, they will go. I think that it is finally incumbent upon us in English-speaking Canada to take a new look at the Quebec fact and at the French fact in that province.
1 should like to draw an historical analogy with events in the United States. I realize that when one becomes involved in historical analogies there is always the problem that the facts do not fit together completely. But let us cast our minds back to the United States in the 1850's. When I was in high school I was taught that slavery was the major issue in the war between the states, but if one reads those American historians who give more weight to the economic situation at the time, one finds that slavery was not the cause, or the major cause, of the war of secession. It was the politicizing of slavery, the extension of slavery into the territories in the west, the states of Kansas, Nebraska and so on.
The American constitution lays it down that each state shall have two senators, regardless of the size of its population. When it became clear to the political leaders of the south, many of whom had begun to free their slaves, that it was no longer financially and materially profitable for them to remain within the union, when it became clear that they had lost their balance of power in the United States Senate, it was then and then only that they decided to secede. 1 believe there is an analogy there.
1 believe French-speaking Quebecers feel today that it is no longer financially, materially and politically advantageous for them to remain within the present structure of Confederation. But have we heard from the Prime Minister on this question? When the travelling circus-pardon me, the travelling caucus-was in Brantford, was anything discussed there by any of the three cabinet ministers or any of the three Liberal MPs along these lines? Did they address themselves to this great national issue? No, Mr. Speaker. The Minister of Public Works (Mr. Buchanan) got the headlines in the Brantford Expositor. They were to the effect that the government might

October 27, 1977
The Address-Mr. H. Gray
tamper with the old age security program and cut back children's allowances.
I say to hon. members on the other side, as a matter of interest to them, that it would have been better had the Liberal travelling circus, or caucus, not gone to Brantford. No important national issue was discussed there. They came to listen, and all they did was talk. That is not the way to enter into a dialogue with constituents. I have not heard of them travelling to ridings represented by Liberal members, though 1 could be wrong.
The unity issue in this country is tied in directly with the economic prospect facing us. Unless and until we can come to grips with unemployment, with job insecurity which causes emotional instability, nervous breakdowns, disruption of families, and juvenile delinquency, it will be extremely difficult to resolve. All of these flow from economic problems plaguing the nation.
1 am very happy to see the Minister of Finance enter the Chamber. He is a busy man these days and he personally is a very likable man. But unless he can come up with something a little more innovative, a little more creative and dynamic, something which comes more from the heart than just the mind, then what he said last Thursday night is not going to solve our basic economic problems. It is not going to solve the unemployment crisis. We already have on record the fact that it did not work with Mr. Turner's budget, and it did not work with the budget of the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Macdonald). Yet we are getting the same dose of medicine for the same disease.
I love my country, Mr. Speaker. I do not want to see it break up. I do not want to see divisiveness in the west or in Quebec or in the maritimes. But when you consider that in a riding such as Brant, in the so-called affluent part of Canada, southwestern Ontario, the real unemployment rate is around 11 per cent, the highest since the great depression, and when you consider the unemployment rate in parts of New Brunswick, Newfoundland, Cape Breton Island and the northern areas of our country, is it little wonder that people are asking why they should even bother to go out and vote on election day? They ask: "What is the point? Can they do anything? Will the government do anything?"
These are fundamental questions which we have to ask ourselves. We have to come to grips with our problems in this country in a spirit of unity. In summation, we in Ottawa have to create an environment in which Quebec City is just as important a provincial capital as Regina, Victoria, Toronto or any of the other provincial capitals. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, we are not going to do it with the stroke of a pen on a legal or constitutional document; it has to come from the government-from us-directly to the Canadian people. Whether we are Francophone or Anglophone, we must work together.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the throne speech speaks of "the urgent need for important structural

adjustments' in the Canadian economy. The prices and incomes controls program, which began some two years ago, was intended to provide a breathing space for the government to put in place, "structural policies to ensure a more efficient and competitive economy". These were the words of the white paper entitled "Attack on Inflation" which the government tabled when the controls program was first announced.
The date for a phased out ending of controls, April 14 of next year, has finally been announced by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien), and this means that that breathing space provided by the controls will soon be ending. Yet there is a tremendous amount to be done to make Canada a more efficient economy, one which is more competitive both here and abroad. The government must use the time remaining while the controls continue to apply to deal with the structural problems in question, even though it is clear that much will remain to be done after the controls have gone.
In the white paper tabled just before the October, 1976, throne speech entitled "The Way Ahead", the government spoke of the need to improve and strengthen competition policy as a way of bringing about needed structural change in the market place. The government made it clear in that white paper that it would be relying primarily on the market system as a means of enabling Canadians to achieve their economic and social goals.
Another government policy paper, "Agenda for Co-operation", was published earlier this year, and it too stressed the importance for a post-controls society of a complete reform of competition policy. In addition, it stressed the importance of implementing the borrowers' and depositors' protection act to improve the operation of the market place for credit and to strike at the loan sharking operations that tarnish the market place and harm consumers generally.
The stage two competition bill was given first reading this year. Its subject matter was studied by the finance committee, which issued a detailed report of its findings and recommendations. The borrowers' and depositors' protection act received second reading and was in the final stages of committee consideration when the session adjourned.
In light of the importance that these measures have in terms of bringing about the needed structural changes in the market place, I think it is disturbing that they are not mentioned at all in the Speech from the Throne. It is true that earlier this week the present Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Allmand), in a speech outside the House, said that these bills would be reintroduced. However, one can wonder as to the implications of the failure to mention these two important measures in any way in the throne speech itself. Certainly a reference to them in the speech would have confirmed the commitment by the government as a whole to implement these two key measures, measures which are vital to the effective operation of the market place and to the well-being of business and consumers alike.
Government and business spokesmen have been saying that uncertainty has been hampering the development of business confidence necessary for the recovery of the economy. I think
October 27, 1977

the lack of final parliamentary decisions on these two measures helps to add to the very uncertainty the government wishes to eliminate. Perhaps the government is holding back because of what appears to be the developing and seemingly well orchestrated campaign whereby certain elements express the views of the largely big business sector of the economy in opposition to these bills. They argue that these measures would hamper the proper operation of the market place; they argue that they are among the factors convincing some Canadian businessmen to invest in the United States and in other foreign countries rather than Canada.
These are strange arguments, Mr. Speaker. They are wrong arguments. They turn reality upside down. The two bills are not designed to be the instruments for improper government interference or over-regulation of an already properly operating market place. Instead, they are aimed at ensuring its effective operation in the interests of all Canadians, a market place which is free from domination by a few large firms. Surely enabling the proper operation of market forces is exactly what those opposing the adoption of the bill are supposed to favour.
In addition, those who say that the proposed competition policy is encouraging them to invest in the United States are talking about going to a country whose present anti-trust laws, their competition laws, are already tougher and more bureaucratically interventionist than anything proposed by the government in the stage two competition policy bill. In fact all of the western countries, even that bastion of free enterprise, West Germany, have been updating and tightening their competition laws.
But it is not correct that all business generally opposes the bills 1 have been talking about, especially the stage two bill. The Canadian Federation of Independent Business and the National Automotive Trades Association, for example, are the legitimate voices of broad segments of the business community. They support the stage two bill and are calling for its early implementation.
The government's resolve, its sincerity in getting on with completing the long delayed reform of competition policy and the equally much needed updating of the federal consumer credit law, will not be demonstrated just by the early reintroduction of these two bills. More important, this resolve and sincerity will be demonstrated by the government through its giving the necessary priority on the agenda of parliament to moving them along to the final stages of decision-making as soon as possible. I am not saying, in doing this, that valid points for the improvement of the two bills made by business and consumer groups during their original consideration in the last session should be ignored. These points can and should be dealt with; but this can be done and the bills be moved along without delay to their final adoption and implementation.
The passing of these two measures will serve the best interests of all those businessmen who really believe what so many of them have been preaching about the market system.
The Address-Mr. H. Gray
It will serve the best interests of consumers and small business in particular but, more important, it will serve the best interests of Canadians generally.
Food was another structural problem area raised by the 1975 "Attack on Inflation" white paper. The Speech from the Throne has a section dealing with the implementation of the government's food strategy. This strategy appeared to have been set out in the policy paper entitled "A Food Strategy for Canada", tabled jointly by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) and the then minister of consumer and corporate affairs last June. It set out what the government considered to be "the basic principles of a food strategy for Canada to assure all Canadians that its policies and programs ensure adequate supplies of safe and nutritious foods at prices which are reasonable to both producers and consumers." In doing so, it admitted that "in the past principles and procedures have not been used to co-ordinate all relevant elements of Canada's food policy."
With few exceptions, little was said in the paper about specific operating programs to implement the strategy. One of the specific pledges in it was that the government will ensure "in any appointments to boards and agencies ... the views of producers, processors and consumers are adequately represented." Another was that the government "will provide regular price information to consumers on a selected set of basic foods." But nothing whatsoever has been done since last June to put into place, or even to announce formally, these two programs or any of the others specifically set out or hinted at in the strategy document. However, they did resurface in identical form in the throne speech. It also promised that a national food conference would be held, although it is not clear to what extent the implementation of the two specific programs I mentioned are linked to that conference first having taken place.
The throne speech indicates that the conference " will bring together representatives of governments, producers, consumers and food industry to work together toward a national agreement on how Canada's food strategy should be further developed and implemented." The House should bear in mind that the objectives for food strategy I have quoted from the government document of last June appeared in rather similar terms in the February, 1974, throne speech over three years ago. That was the one that was presented not long before the 1974 general election. In that throne speech the objectives are described as being a "policy on food" which "the government is developing." At best, the process of development seems to have been and continues to be rather slow and laborious.
The February, 1974, throne speech indicated that "the government will wish to consult with provincial governments, consumer groups and producers" in developing its food policy. This was what was said in 1974. Yet the Minister of Agriculture recently announced that the national food conference finally promised in the current throne speech will not take place until next February. He has called for briefs from various organizations to be submitted to the government by December. He said that certain of the organizations presenting

The Address-Mr. H. Gray
briefs will be allowed to discuss them with a panel of ministers in December. He said that this panel will be drawn from among a number of ministers including the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. What is surprising about this announcement is that it would appear from it that the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs will not be allowed, as a matter of course, to be involved in each and every discussion. This means the cabinet representative of the voice of individual Canadians as consumers will be absent from some of these important discussions this coming December.
In 1973 the House of Commons set up, at the government's request, a special all-party committee on food price trends. It heard witnesses from all areas of the food system. Also in that year the government created the Food Prices Review Board. Its members represented not just consumers but manufacturers, producers, and business as well. Both of these bodies issued extensive reports proposing changes and improvements in food policy. So the government has already had before it for some time results of a consultative process involving these two organizations. These reports will likely cover much of the same ground as one could expect would be covered by the food conference. In any event, it would not be fully realistic to expect producers, consumers and manufacturers to agree on a single program which all sides would consider equally fair to them in every possible respect.
Consultation is a necessary and worth-while part of working out government policies in a country like Canada. But in areas where complete agreement by all parties to be affected by government policies is not possible, the government has a responsibility to show leadership and to take action in the over-all interest of the public. Therefore I hope, if the national agreement sought by the government does not prove to be possible, that the government will not use its absence as an excuse for delaying meaningful action to put in place necessary elements of a true, comprehensive food policy.
It is interesting to see the recent efforts by the Minister of Agriculture to promote his department as the new protector of the consumer in the food area; but even with the re-organization he has recently announced, it is likely going to be a long time before it has any real credibility for this purpose in the eyes of most consumers as being able, and in fact willing, to deal fairly with their interests.
Also nothing was said in his speech in the House yesterday specifically about providing foods "at prices which are reasonable to consumers" as a component of the agricultural development strategy he was outlining as an obviously necessary and desirable part of a total food strategy. Yet these words which were absent from his speech are an important part of what the government said last June were its objectives for food strategy. Instead, in his speech, the minister spoke of stable prices. This is not necessarily the same thing as reasonable prices. The best interests of both consumers and producers will be served if the government puts in place measures to provide prices for them which are at one and the same time stable and reasonable. That is not an easy task, to be sure, but one which should be among the overriding objectives of a national food strategy. I

October 27, 1977
would hope the promises of consultation in a national food conference will not turn out to be excuses for government inaction.
Turning to the matter of the economy generally, regretfully I have doubts that the tax cuts announced by the Minister of Finance last week will do much to add to consumer demand and reduce our chronic and all too high level of unemployment in any substantive way. The Minister of Finance has in fact tightened up the guideline for allowable wage increases for the period of the controls program just begun. The government will not be allowing wages to increase sufficiently to keep in step with the actual degree to which inflation has exceeded 6 per cent, contrary to the promise it made to workers that it would do this kind of thing when the controls program was first announced. Therefore, the tax cut will not be likely to give consumers a sufficient degree of additional buying power. Instead it will be cancelled by the tighter wage guidelines.
The size of the deficit obviously provides constraints on what the government might be able to do, but surely government efforts to stimulate the economy would have the effect of reducing the deficit rather than increasing it. Government programs stimulating the economy, which got people back to productive work, would mean much less money being paid out by the government for unemployment insurance, welfare and the like than at present. Also the government would gain more tax revenues, not only from workers back in productive jobs, but also from business as it increases its activity.
I think the government before too long will have to do more than was announced last Thursday to stimulate the buying power of Canadians and generally to get the economy moving.
I will abbreviate my remarks somewhat because of the order adopted by the House earlier today to limit the time of speeches to 20 minutes, but it is my intention to release my notes as a statement of my views on those areas on which I will not comment in detail today. I hope they will prove to be of interest to members of the House and to the public generally. Also I should like to say that my comments, as always, are being made in a constructive sense. I am making them as a Liberal, someone who supports the government, believing it is certainly preferable to the alternatives, but also as someone who wants it to be a Liberal government not just in name but in policy orientation and action, in the belief that this is the desire of most Canadians as well.
I have been talking about structural problems. The ultimate challenge to the federal government and to all of us is to preserve and to improve the structure of Canada itself as a united country. The throne speech, as I and others have been pointing out since last November should be the case, recognizes that the economy and national unity are not separate issues, that they are closely intertwined. As I have been saying, the ability of the federal government, our national government, to show that it can deal effectively with problems such as the economy, that are real to people everywhere in Canada, helps to demonstrate the value of having one country for Quebecers
October 27, 1977

and all Canadians. This means that the federal government must show leadership in dealing with economic and social problems which, if unsolved, can call into question in the minds of people in some parts of the country the value of being part of a united Canada. It means ensuring through federal government leadership and action that all can feel, and in fact will be, equally at home in this country whether they are French-speaking or English-speaking, and this must include both the French language minority groups outside of Quebec and the English language minority group in that province.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: It means federal government leadership and action to bring about changes and adjustments where necessary to our federal structure aimed at improving its functioning in a way that recognizes regional and other differences, but which does not weaken that structure to the extent that we no longer have in fact one country. Finally, it means the strong efforts of all of us here in this House of Commons and all of us who believe in a united Canada, not just to preserve it but to improve it, to preserve and improve our country so as to bring about the development of its potential, both material and human, in the best interests of all its people.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to speak in this debate and to contribute my point of view both for the record and for the consideration of people in Canada.
I would like to extend traditional greetings of good will to the mover and seconder of the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne and to wish them and the new members who were elected in the by-elections success in their role as members of parliament.
As a westerner I am especially happy that the Queen was able to open this parliament. Also, as a westerner I have long been of the opinion that the monarchy has played an important role in this century in tying together the many ethnic groups which have come to the West, particularly in the first part of this century.
There are those who may have said cynically that perhaps if Louis Riel and his dream of a republic on the prairies had succeeded, we might now have been better off, but 1 must say that I believe in the monarchy and that the role of British insitutions has been important in binding western Canada to Confederation, at least in the early part of this century. I think the considerable divisiveness that has occurred in the country has been the result of the loss of symbols that monarchy has represented. The British empire has disappeared and the British nation no longer plays the role that it previously played in the world, but until a few decades ago it still represented a bulwark against the south. It may be said that some of our failures and the divisiveness which we are experiencing in Canada today might be the result of our failure to create new symbols to replace the old.
Now before I should like to turn to the issue of national unity and the economy and to express two concerns of a
The Address-Mr. Ritchie
regional nature, one affecting my riding especially. The first one to which I will refer is with regard to the failure of the Department of the Environment to establish in the town of Swan River a meteorological office which has been promised for the last ten years. For some reason, while the government expends vast sums of money in many ways on such programs as language training, it fails to provide the basic structure on which communities exist.
The area of Swan River in my riding has no adequate weather forecasting service because the present stations are located too far away. Weather conditions there are variable. This area needs a weather forecasting station in particular because its geographic location places it on the borderline between the weather systems from the northwest Alaska and weather systems from the western United States. Small aircraft, in particular, need more adequate weather forecasting in this area than is being provided at present. The Department of the Environment has demonstrated a cavalier attitude for the last ten years in regularly including the establishment of such a station in the area in its estimates, only to change its mind at the last minute. This has made the citizens in the area feel that they are being discriminated against by the Ottawa bureaucracy.
There is one other subject of a somewhat parochial nature which I should like to talk about, that is, the matter of the grading of wheat under the new grading rules of the Canadian Grain Commission. It has become obvious now that the new grading system heavily favours those areas of the prairies that grow the so-called No. 1 Hard Red spring wheat to the detriment of areas such as the Parkland regions in the prairies where a lower protein quality of wheat is grown. The recent long wet spell has reduced the quality of much of the wheat grown in the Parkland region to No. 3 utility, and there is a large spread between No. 3 Red and No. 3 utility, amounting to 50 cents a bushel. This is causing great concern and unhappiness among the growers.
The new grading system which allows for only three grades in the Canada west red variety applies only to top quality wheat, and it seems that all other grades of wheat are to be consigned to No. 3 utility. Under the old grading system there were six grades of wheat and one grade of feed wheat, which allowed for a price spread differential between all grades. It is obvious that on occasion the Parkland area particularly will produce mostly No. 3 utility wheat. It seems that the Wheat Board finds it convenient not to have to deal with as many grades as it did formerly.
Certainly the new grading system makes it easier for the Wheat Board to sell grain because it does not need to deal with the number of grades which existed under the previous grading system. Furthermore, the introduction of the new grading system means that in effect the Wheat Board, which is a selling agency, does not need to deal with lower grades of millable wheat. It prefers to sell merely No. 3 utility at feed wheat prices, although, on occasion, much of this grain will enter the markets of the world as millable wheat. This means a considerable loss to growers, amounting to tens of millions of

dollars, if not hundreds of million of dollars. The Board of Grain Commissioners should consider adding a fourth grade of grain between No. 3 red and No. 3 utility.
I believe that this grading system of wheat discourages farmers from growing wheat in the Parkland area in particular, and over a period of time it could seriously discourage the production of wheat in these areas. Therefore 1 think this matter should be resolved by the Board of Grain Commissioners and the Canadian Wheat Board.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the dinner hour I was about to discuss the economic condition of our country. After nine years of this government under the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) we have severe economic conditions; we have the problems of high inflation, high unemployment, and diminished economic activity. That we should be in this situation had been foreseen for a long time. We are not entirely alone in this situation, as witness the problems of the United Kingdom, France, Italy, and our neighbour to the south.
Essentially inflation will occur when governments overspend. Governments do little in the way of production, but they are always happy to promote spending and to see the production of workers in society expanded. The vast expansion of governments in particular fields where governments have declared an interest, such as health, education, and welfare, has really meant that a large number of people have been taking, and this problem has grown to the monster it is now so that it is threatening the economic base of the country.
Perhaps we could keep going on this course more easily if the energy crisis had not come along. It is obvious that much of the advance in affluence in countries around the world was based on cheap oil and energy prices. As the availability of cheap energy comes to an end-it is now essentially under the control of the Arab nations which are intent on making the best use of their good fortunes-we are witnessing an abrupt end to the continuing expansion of the good life we have had for the past 25 years.

The Prime Minister has suggested that even though Canadians have developed a high standard of living over the past 25 years they are more unhappy and more disunited than ever before, and he wonders why. I agree that per capita it can be shown that Canadians are about twice as well off as they were 25 years ago. Perhaps it is a very human reaction that when there are good times, regardless of productivity, individuals in society do not relate their good fortunes to the productivity of their fellow workers but regard affluence as a happening to which they are entitled.
Twenty-five years ago the role of government was much simpler. When governments involved themselves in the fields of health, welfare, and education, it was at the local level, and citizens were very much more aware of the true cost of the services they received. The involvement of the government in our social programs has created uncontrolled expenditure, and the end is not yet in sight. The federal government has involved itself in hospitalization, medical care, drug care, social security and, to a lesser extent, education, to the point that reasonable prudence is not being observed. Furthermore, vast amounts of taxation come to Ottawa and are then redistributed to the regions, and this only heightens the divisiveness within Canada.
In today's Globe and Mail Mr. Ronald Anderson has this to
say:
Real incomes rose strongly and it became economically possible and politically necessary for politicians to improve the quality of social services and to work toward a fairer distribution of incomes.
These social measures-in the fields, for example, of pensions, health care, education, unemployment insurance and other transfer payments-may well have created an inflationary bias. Probably public sector activity increased too rapidly. But this is an area in which there is considerable room for debate. The question is not whether improvement in social programs was needed, but whether the structure, scale and timing of the new measures were appropriate.
I think it can be said that the federal government must take the blame for many of these programs that were pushed too fast.
The malaise that affects our economy will not soon go away, because we have spent 30 years creating the situation we now face. During the past 30 years we have had a change of attitude and a change of circumstances within our society so far as the individual is concerned. An individual in the past had to be prudent; he saved money for his old age because he was expected to look after himself. But now things are changed. At the present time an individual can have a modest living from the old age pension and the supplement and Canada Pension, unless he is in peculiar circumstances. He finds that from the cradle to the grave there is no need to worry about paying physicians for health care or paying hospitals for hospital care. All of these are provided by the state out of general revenue. Is it any wonder that people are providing themselves with holidays in far-away places?
With the inflation the way it is, the value savings in mortgages, bonds and bank accounts is being halved every few years. Some would say this may well be a change in our society's structure and that we are in the post industrial state.
October 27, 1977

Then again, there is the media's view of what politicians should do as regards spending programs. A politician who votes against the major spending programs is regarded as negative or lacking in compassion, while the politician who votes for vast government social enterprises is regarded as positive or compassionate. What is positive about a government that runs a national deficit of over $9 billion and prints money to finance it? What is positive or compassionate about a constant inflation rate of 8 per cent to 10 per cent, a rate at which half of an individual's life savings is destroyed every eight years? What is positive about a government whose regulations cost consumers billions of dollars each year? And what is positive about a government that is printing money at a rate almost twice as fast as the rate that the nation's economy is growing? We need a rethinking of our economic and political structure in this country.
Now, Mr. Speaker, this leads into what I would like to say and what is beginning to emerge in discussions about the future of this country. There seems to be a general agreement that there needs to be a re-arranging to the federal-provincial powers for all the regions if this diverse country is to function. It has been pointed out by some that we are already a fairly decentralized country. Mr. Speaker, before the federal government assumed a high portion of the social costs in the last 25 years we had quite a decentralized country and we functioned reasonably effectively. The fall of the Canadian dollar, obscured and cushioned by the precipitous fall of the American dollar, points up the serious economic conditions in which this country finds itself. The mere fact that today the Canadian dollar was at its lowest in 45 years only indicates the gravity of the situation.
Speaking of regions, Mr. Speaker, an article in the Manitoba Co-operator of March 20, 1977, referring to The Financial Post 'Think West' Conference Edmonton recently had this to say about regions:
There has to be a new deal for Confederation. Lougheed puts it this way when he says change is necessary "but it can't be legalistic, it can't be tied in with the constitution. It must be a matter of attitude and spirit and co-operation-not a legal document. It can't have special status for any one province, but it must recognize that provinces are different and that each should have the opportunity to find its way in the areas that are important to it".
The strain on national unity makes the revival of Canada's industrial activity an urgent priority-and the location for new efforts should be dictated by economic imperatives, not traditional habit.
But, Mr. Speaker, if the economic situation is grave, the political situation can only be described as disastrous. The Prime Minister seems to be getting ready to run on the favourable Liberal wheelhorse that only the Liberal government can guarantee Canadian unity. Let us look at the history of this contention. Since 1896, when Sir Wilfrid Laurier assumed power in Canada, the Liberal party has governed for 60 years. Only on three short occasions was the Conservative party in power, while on two occasions during this time there were serious political problems facing the country. The first was the First World War that taxed the resources of Canada to the utmost, and the second was the great depression.
The Address-Mr. Ritchie
Furthermore, during that time the province of Quebec contributed three Prime Ministers whose tenure of office spread over some 35 years. It has been recognized by political adversaries that the province of Quebec, through solemnly supporting the Liberal party for a century, has had a major say in the direction that the government of this country has taken. So strong is the feeling of western Canadians that the government of this country has been dominated by the wishes of central Canada that they have become alienated and have less than absolute loyalties to the Canadian state.
The passage of the bilingual law which had the effect of closing to unilingual people in the civil service, the armed forces, the RCMP through language requirements, the normal advancement that they might expect, has created violent animosities in that part of Canada that might have been sympathetic and viewed favourably the Canadian experience. Yet it is that part of Canada that has had the most influence in shaping the government of our country that is now demanding that separation take place. Certainly there are problems with any nation with two languages and any nation that tries to give them equal status. It seems to me that Belgium is an example of a small country that has attempted to solve its language problem by separating the two language groups.
English-speaking Canada has largely been a bystander in this debate that is in progress and that is looming for the future. Why has French Canada a monopoly on this issue, whether it is federalist or separatist in nature? Part of it is a recognition by many English Canadians that, given the circumstances, it will be up to the Quebecers to decide the future of Quebec. Anyone who thinks differently might consider the reaction in the Quebec National Assembly to the suggestion of the Prime Minister that there be a referendum. All parties opposed to the Parti Quebecois in that legislature consider themselves federalists and oppose Quebec independence, but they seem to have rallied behind Quebec's right to decide its own future. Frustration and anger are growing in English Canada at the long debate, particularly within a province that seems to have gained greatly in its political and economic status by belonging to the Canadian federation. Furthermore, it is obvious that there is growing in the rest of Canada not more spirit of compromise but a greater spirit of antagonism.
The Prime Minister in the Speech from the Throne said that we should press forward with greater language training in the second official language. Well, the second official language has been available for years, even in my maligned province of Manitoba and, as one who had studied that language, French, to gain an entrance to university, 1 can attest that there has always been second training available. Incidentally, it was the first Quebec Prime Minister of Canada, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, who approved in fact the actions of the government of Manitoba in 1894, and it was the federal Conservative government of Sir Mackenzie Bowell which was readying legislation to remedy the situation and that was filibustered by the Liberals under Sir Wilfrid Laurier so that the legislation was never passed.

Those who think second language training will make a material difference to the Canadian unity problem, I think are sadly mistaken. Facility in the use of second languages in the majority of the population only comes about when there is a need to speak two languages. Therefore, in the sea of English in North America, to expect that by offering language training in schools in English-speaking provinces there will be a great espousing of the French language is unrealistic.
During the debate on the Speech from the Throne the Prime Minister indicated that he would set up legislation to allow for referendums for various possible political decisions. Mr. Speaker, I would like to remind the House that the hon. member for Palliser (Mr. Schumacher), seconded by me, introduced private member's Bill C-412, called "An Act Respecting the Holding of a National Plebiscite on the Separation of Quebec from Canada".
Referendums have serious disadvantages. Even in the province of Quebec it could be that a federal referendum might turn those who are not disposed to independence toward that goal if they felt that the national federalism were steamrolling their province. Furthermore, a federal referendum would have little effect on the outcome of a referendum in the province of Quebec alone. It has always been assumed that a national unity referendum would show an overwhelming majority of Canadians in other provinces are for the maintenance of the Canadian federation, as we learned in the referendum on conscription in 1942. This great outpouring of good will has been generated in English Canada from churches. Chambers of Commerce, and professional groups.
Everyone outside Quebec suggests that he loves Canada and wants Quebec to remain because they are cherished and needed. However, there is a substantial group in English Canada, perhaps still a minority, but in my estimation perhaps as large a group as 25 per cent, and in certain areas as large as 50 per cent-

Looking at some of the speeches that have been made, 1 note that the hon. member for Don Valley (Mr. Gillies) made a very interesting comment. At page 48 he was reported to have said:
The only organization that can live beyond its means in this country is the federal government.
Surely the hon. member with his stature and recognition as an economist knows better than that. He went on to say:
The myth that has been spread that innation in this country has been caused by people wanting too much, by unions demanding too much, by corporations demanding too much, is wrong.
The hon. member who professes to be an economist says it is a myth that unions and management demanding too much contribute to inflation, that the only one responsible is the federal government. According to that, no responsibility is needed on the part of those making wage demands, demands which in fact were 22 per cent before the AIB took over. Would a resurgence of strikes which have fallen off by more than 63 per cent from this time last year be all right to the hon. member for Don Valley after the AIB controls come off April 14? Would he leave it solely up to the federal government to be responsible for some of the concessions made prior to AIB?
This government is restraining public service salaries, having them follow, not lead, salaries in the private sector. That, to me, puts on private sector management, and on unions, the onus for wage restraint, especially after the controls end. For too long, before controls came in, too much of management did not negotiate hard enough, because they would either pass on increases to consumers or they would look to government to step in. During controls, they could shelter under the control levels. They can do that for a little while, but not much longer. Then there will be a heavy onus on firms to negotiate hard and, at times, to hang tough. The hon. member for Don Valley does not accept this as a responsibility. He wishes that off on the federal government.

In any event, to go on, we recognize we are in serious times, times of soft markets abroad and accelerated, even cut-throat competition internationally. Prices and costs are still too high here and productivity is too low. There are many problems, but 1 will mention four which are basic to the Canadian economy. Put simply, there are vastly more goods competing on the markets of the world than there were even four or five years ago. World industrial capacity, especially with respect to manufactured products, has grown enormously-from the EEC and especially from the Japanese and German economies, from developing countries pouring out goods produced by labour and under easier environmental rules. We have to be very sophisticated in our products as well as price-competitive in order to compete-and that means here in our home markets as well as abroad.
Increased foreign industrial capacity can be a strength for Canada. We are geared to supplying that capacity not only with primary and processed products but also with manufactured and capital goods for other industries. Thus, world economic slowdown hits hard at our trading economy. But we should be poised to capitalize on international recovery.
Another important factor is that Canada's population growth is levelling out and immigration is slowing down. This should reduce the underlying pressure for domestic growth. We can see the results of this in certain sectors already, such as education, some areas of health care, housing, and in connection with products for use by the young. I do not wish to make too much of this aspect. We still are going to need, and will sustain, a significant growth rate in the years ahead. But we may not, and we should not, expect to get back to the extremely high growth rate of the 1950's and 1960's. What I am saying is that when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) forecasts a growth rate for next year of 5 per cent, the knee-jerk reaction should not be that this is a sluggish rate. Such a rate will be good going, and I pray we can keep it up year after year.

October 27, 1977
The Address-Mr. Horner
The third basic problem facing Canada is the rapid increase in costs and the consequent drop, over the last three or four years, in our ability to compete. This government, to be frank, protected Canadians against world-wide price increases for energy, for some foods and for certain industrial commodities. Canadians tried to protect themselves by raising their incomes as fast as, or faster than, prices.
As a result, wage rates climbed as high as, or higher than those in the United States, with productivity 15 to 20 per cent lower. We sold less abroad and this resulted in giant deficits along with huge interest payments. Even worse, the situation led to increasing inroads into our own domestic markets by imports.
The fourth and most dramatic problem has been the well-recognized revolution in oil prices and its particular effect on energy-intensive western economies.
Just as 1 have not tried to gloss over our situation, Mr. Speaker, neither should it be painted hopelessly black. All those problem situations I referred to-the other industrialized nations face them as well. In a depressed and psychologically shell-shocked world we have performed remarkably well. We have a sound foundation on which to build.
Since 1973 Canadian manufacturing output has held up much better than in most western economies. It declined in the period 1973-1975 by 2.5 per cent. But in the United States the decline was 10 per cent; in Japan it was 14 per cent, and it was almost 9 per cent in West Germany. Manufacturing now accounts for about 20 per cent of total Canadian production as compared to between 22 and 24 per cent for the years 195173, a drop precisely the same as that which took place in the United States and other countries where the services sector is going ahead. Productivity over the 25 years to 1975 consistently narrowed the giant gap between ourselves and the United States. We slipped back in 1976, but are gaining again this year. Manufactured exports still pay for 80 per cent of the manufactured goods we import so heavily. In terms of over-all economic growth, only Japan and Germany, recovering from very low levels of post-war industrial activity, have better over-all records.
Improvements and opportunities exist to allow us to build on our good base. First, Canadian wages and costs are now growing no more rapidly than in the U.S. We have not recovered the ground lost in the last three years, but the gap is not getting any worse. Indeed it is narrowing. Second, the lower Canadian dollar helps our competitive position. It does raise the cost of our imports, but at least it helps our sales if we do not fritter away this helpful reprieve through a further round of wage and cost increase. That is why I was so shocked to hear the hon. member for Don Valley suggest that as far as those responsible for demands on wages are concerned it was all up to the government. I was shocked to hear him say this, because we cannot afford to fritter away the gains we have made in this regard. We must continue to make what I would call long term gains in productivity as compared with the United States. This will take a long time, perhaps, but we are on our way back and should do well.

Third, the lifting of controls over the next year will remove an element of uncertainty from business by bringing the market system back into place in the determination of prices and wages. It is under these conditions that business can best be relied upon to generate the capital necessary for expansion and increased activities. I hope that when controls come off on April 14 they will be followed by a monitoring device which will encourage business and the unions to adopt a far more responsible attitude than the hon. member for Don Valley has suggested.
Fourth, governments in Canada have got their houses in better order. Federal government expenditures have been held to the growth rate of the GNP. Public service hiring is under one per cent. Even in the face of high unemployment, new money for job creation was found within the existing budget. Public sector wages are not any more leading private sector averages for similar skills.
In the midst of unemployment and continuing inflation, then, Canada is in a better position, presently and potentially, than one would imagine from the excess of gloom around. What is needed is business confidence in our basic advantages if we streamline, modernize, cut costs, specialize, and work hard. We need to restructure, adjust, merge, and tighten up. We need to upgrade our resources and negotiate better markets for them, whether they be petrochemicals, beef exported to the United States, grain exported almost everywhere. Fisheries and forest products can be sold abroad and within this country. On all of these things the federal government is now working.
