Mr. Speaker, it is a great pleasure and privilege for me to participate in today's debate. I want to join with all previous speakers in commending the mover and seconder of the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne, the hon. member for Louis-Hebert (Mr. Dawson), and the hon. member for Malpeque (Mr. Wood).
This throne speech, delivered in a most excellent, capable and graceful manner by Her Majesty Queen Elizabeth, even in complimentary terms can only be described as a vague and feeble attempt to revive the government's sagging fortunes. The government has seized upon a moment of great public attention to make excuses for itself and to point the finger of blame at everybody and everything in sight. Indeed, the only impressive thing about the throne speech is the fact that it was given by Her Majesty and presented in truly a magnificent fashion.
Given the record of this government and the attention, or more accurately the lack of attention, given to the throne speech proclamations, one comes to the conclusion that its
October 27, 1977

contents are really meaningless. The speech is a form of window dressing which only momentarily lifts the hopes and aspirations of Canadians. You cannot, under any circumstances, hope to maintain the trust of people by completely ignoring their problems or difficulties, or by continuously taking the attitude that governments are always right and that the people are always wrong. This government has been so wrong on so many occasions, on so many issues, during the years of its administration.
Last Wednesday my colleague and leader led off this debate in a manner in keeping with his traditional debating excellence. He spoke with knowledge, compassion, and understanding, and addressed his remarks squarely to the issues and problems perplexing Canada and bothering Canadians today. He spoke eloquently about the great gift and the great opportunity given this government and this Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) when taking office.
What has happened and what has developed since that time under this government's administration, Mr. Speaker, is really nothing short of a national disaster and, speaking in human terms, a national disgrace. Phrases like "separation is dead", "national unity will be achieved", "the land is strong , "the just society", "inflation will be wrestled to the ground"-and the list goes on-are simply cliches, hackneyed phrases, empty words which only hold out false hopes for Canadians.
1 have with me, with the compliments of my colleague from the riding of Norfolk-Hildimand (Mr. Knowles), recorded excerpts from a well respected newspaper which are typical of many which appeared immediately after the 1968 general election. This particular one is dated the day after, June 26, 1968, and the headline reads "Canadian Unity Assured". The lead line of the editorial begins: "That above all is the meaning of yesterday's election". A typical paragraph reads:
So we shall have a Liberal government for the next few years led by a tuned in, turned on intellectual who must demonstrate he can wield together a cabinet of diverse personalities, administer a government and resolve the country's problems of national unity and of economic stability and develop its human and regional resources.
The words of that editorial, written some nine and a half years ago, held out, 1 must admit, great expectations, and reflected to a very large extent the feeling of Canadians of that day. But if Canadians would simply judge the performance of this government by its record-and I am certain that they will, given the opportunity-then its members, and particularly those who are members of the cabinet, would go to the foot of the line, to the bottom of the class.
It is true that the government has, during its term of office, established many records-record inflation, the highest in the country's history and still rising; record unemployment, higher than in the great depression and still rising; record spending, with a total budget of somewhere in the vicinity of $48 billion and the government still spending; a record deficit which will be somewhere in the vicinity of $9 billion, an amount greater than the total budget at the time this government took office in 1968 under the same leadership it has today. In addition we have an 89 cent dollar, the lowest value since the 1930's and the product of a weak, high cost, underproductive economy.
The Address-Mr. Wise
It is not my intention or my wish to quarrel with some of the tax measures brought forth last Thursday evening by the newest Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien). Indeed, many such measures had been requested for months by members on this side of the House. But I doubt, Mr. Speaker, given the present high degree of uncertainty, that they will provide a sufficient incentive for investors, business and industry to respond as they would wish.
I welcome the proposal to provide tax credits to the private sector for the purpose of job creation. Indeed I firmly believe that the job retraining and apprenticeship programs should even be expanded. One area that the government is neglecting to recognize, however, is the cost to the employer of training employees who are on these programs. This cost is extremely substantial and often discourages many employers from participating in such programs.
This is a very important area because, at a time when we have over one million people unemployed, we have in some areas-not in all, but in some-jobs going unfilled. These jobs more often than not are of a skilled or semi-skilled nature. If these programs met the cost of trainee and employer, many of these jobs could be filled and considerable savings would result from not financing Unemployment Insurance Commission benefits, welfare, and other costly social programs.
Further to this, Mr. Speaker, at a time when we have over one million unemployed we are again experiencing the sad and unbelievable situation in which there is a lack of adequate and suitable manpower to harvest many labour intensive farm commodities. Students from our secondary schools and universities, coupled with offshore workers, generally speaking make up the only reliable source of harvest labour. This tells me- and 1 hope it registers with the government-that there is a desperate need to rededicate many Canadians in certain regions to the work ethic and to the imperative need to encourage individual self-motivation. I am happy to see the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) in the House tonight, and I would just remind him that he must totally reject the advice that he will be getting from his officials. He must retain the offshore labour program for as long as this condition exists in Canada.
In the brief time allotted to me I want to bring to the attention of the government a few of the ongoing, or in many cases worsening, problems experienced by the agricultural industry. Let me begin by citing a report from Statistics Canada which indicates that a decline in farm cash receipts occurred in 1976. These were down some $140 million, which means a drop of over 20 per cent. In 1977 it is obvious that farm incomes will again decline. This year's reduction in net farm income could well register a further 10 per cent. For the first eight months farm income is down in British Columbia, it is down in Saskatchewan to the extent of 50 per cent, and it is down in Manitoba, Ontario, Quebec, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island. It is only up slightly in Alberta, and it is up slightly in Nova Scotia. In a brief conversation with the former premier of that province, he indicated that the situation in the province of Nova Scotia really had no way to go but up.

October 27, 1977
The Address-Mr. Wise
In addition to this, I should like to point out that increases in farm input costs far exceed those of farm incomes, and by an ever-increasing margin. Farm operating costs for 1976 jumped by approximately 11 per cent, and another inflationary jump of 10 per cent could be expected this year.
On the subject of farm machinery, a more recent and worrisome statistic is available. Purchases of farm machinery are down by 10 per cent over the past year. For example, in Saskatchewan farm machinery sales have dropped 24 per cent; in Manitoba they have dropped 19 per cent; and Alberta has suffered an 11 per cent reduction as well. These factors have devastating effects on the economies of rural towns and villages throughout the entire country. For example, a 100 horsepower tractor which could be purchased in 1972 for $9,800, now costs around $20,000. A combine priced at $15,000 in 1972 now carries a price tag in excess of $30,000. Diesel fuel has doubled in price during the last five years, and more increases are expected in the future. In the midst of these cost increases, grain prices have decreased sharply, many to the extent of 25 per cent to 50 per cent. Hundreds of other examples could be cited; but whqt is really happening under this government is that farm incomes are sinking and farm input prices are rising. The farm profit margin, if indeed any exists, continues to shrink. It should be obvious to all members that the agricultural producer has the right to a fair return for his investment, labour, management, and his risks.
In a recent speech given by Peter Hannam, the relatively newly elected president of the Ontario Federation of Agriculture, in the city of London, he indicated that a study had been completed by that organization, and the results were that if farmers charged absolutely nothing for their investment, labour, and management-in other words, if they simply donated all the products and commodities they produced-the saving to every consumer would be 23 cents a day. Mr. Speaker, that is less than the price of a cup of coffee or a chocolate bar.
Our fruit and vegetable industries continue to suffer under an antiquated tariff and duty policy. To date there is no indication of acceptance by the government of the Tariff Board report which recommends immediate adjustments and the conversion to an ad valorem system to remove inequities which have existed for over a quarter of a century. There is no indication that seasonal surcharges will be implemented, even when surplus production from outside sources floods Canadian markets and depresses local prices below costs of domestic production. There is no encouraging sign of a government commitment to create an environment for Canadian producers to supply a greater percentage of the domestic market, nor any evidence of aggressive sales programs to expand or seek out new export markets abroad.
We should consider ourselves fortunate as of today that there is no indication that the government intends further studies or inquiries into the beef industry. It has been papered to death. We have had the commission of inquiry and the
(Mr. Wise.]
Senate inquiry-both credible documents-although I question the necessity of public expenditure for the latter. Had the minister the good sense to listen to our recommendations made repeatedly over past months, particularly by the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Hargrave), the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Hurlburt), the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Murta) and others, he could have received his answers and saved Canadian taxpayers and farm organizations over a million dollars and improved the position of those in the agricultural industry, particularly those in the beef industry.
If I could make one point tonight, it would be that 1 want to remind the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) that we have been consistent in our call and recommendations for a Canadian meat import law. In his speech yesterday the minister hinted, after several years of prodding, at the introduction of some similar type of legislation. I say to the minister: bring on your legislation, and if it qualifies in our opinion and measures up to our wishes, and has the teeth to do the job, then we on this side of the House will support it. What further commitment does he require than that? It appears that finally we might have some attention given to the matter of foodland preservation. Although we recognize and respect the fact that this matter is primarily a joint provincial and municipal legislative matter, because of its national importance we continue to urge federal assistance, support and co-operation.
Time does not permit me to deal tonight with such a problem as the explosive situation which exists in the dairy industry, or the ridiculous granting of precious and shamefully inadequate research funds to a former employee and consultant for the Interprovincial Pipeline Company to do a study on the "effects of pipeline construction on the productivity of soils in western Quebec and eastern Ontario." Although such a study is necessary and we would support it without question, this is a scandalous appointment at a cost of nearly $40,000. How can one possibly accept the credibility of the results when the engineer who was hired has testified in courts and supplied information to the courts which has been used against farmers? It is a clear conflict of interest and another prime example of bad judgment and poor judgment on behalf of the government. Peter Lewington, an Ilderton farmer and writer, sums it up accurately by saying, "It's like letting the fox mind the chicken coop".
The Minister of Agriculture in his usual display of buffoonery justified the move of Farm Credit Corporation's head office from Ottawa to Camrose, a move which was purely political. This represents another example of the government's use of power and politics despite the will of the people and the absence of good common sense.
We are concerned about the effects and the results of the recent reorganizational changes in the Department of Agriculture, particularly at a time when a greater flow of information is necessary between the producers, consumers and people in the food industry. The food systems branch created in 1972 to handle this much needed service has been dissolved. Concern has been raised over the possible erosion of authority from the Department of Agriculture to other government departments.
October 27, 1977

For example, there is a current rumour that quality standards and grading could be moved from the Department of Agriculture and shifted to the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs.
We are concerned about the implications of any new competition bill introduced by the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and its effect on the well regulated and adequately supervised orderly marketing systems we have in Canada. What kind of legislation does the minister have in mind when he speaks about consumer representation on all national and provincial marketing boards? Will such members be democratically elected, or will they be unilaterally appointed by the Minister of Agriculture, or perhaps even worse, by the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Allmand)?
We welcome the invitation given by the government for the submission of briefs by the provinces and producer groups leading up to national food strategy conferences in the month of February next year. But we have seen this approach used before, with the end result being that what happens in the formation of policy and the setting of programs is that the government simply imposes its own rights and its own ideas.
To conclude, Mr. Speaker, as I see that my time has almost expired, 1 should like to say that the attention which the government pays to the problems of the agricultural industry in Canada cannot come in sporadic bursts, but rather those problems must be met by far-sighted policies shaped in consultation with those who are directly concerned and directly involved. Unfortunately I do not see any evidence of such a federal commitment, either now or in the foreseeable future, and certainly as long as this government holds office.

Mr. Speaker, I am happy to join in this debate on the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne. 1 want to congratulate the two members who moved the Address in Reply, the hon. member for Louis-Heb-ert (Mr. Dawson) and the hon. member for Malpeque (Mr. Wood). They both acquitted themselves in this debate admirably well for two new young members, just as they did in the by-elections last spring. So 1 congratulate them, as many members of the House have done.
I think this will be a very special session of parliament because, for one thing, it is the first time in some 20 years that Her Majesty has officially opened parliament. She certainly did it with style, grace and elegance, which made it a very special and memorable occasion for all of us. Surely this will likely be the last session of this parliament, so that is another reason for saying it is a very special occasion. The third reason that makes this new session very special, of course, is the fact that for the first time it is being televised, and 1 would like to compliment the government for taking the initiative of bringing television to the House, thus bringing the House closer to the Canadian people and making this place more relevant for Canadians. Someone said recently that this might be called the
The Address-Mr. Foster
"new suit" session of parliament, with everyone getting decked out in their new fancy duds to look great on the new media.
1 think that the throne speech emphasized most properly three areas; the economy, inflation, unemployment and the energy situation in our country. It referred to energy conservation and the development of renewable resources which will be so important in the general energy picture, especially in the future. It mentioned as well the production of gas and oil in the west and in the Arctic. We have had some very encouraging signs this year in the increased production of gas in western Canada. There have been several developments in that regard which, I think, are very encouraging and positive. 1 hope to see the Quebec and maritime natural gas pipeline go ahead, as has been announced during the past few months. Likewise, there is increased interest in gas exploration in the high Arctic islands, and drilling is going forward in the Beaufort Sea. Perhaps the most important energy question that will be before this session of parliament will be legislation relating to the ALCAN pipeline. This is a historic issue which will be put before the House and the Standing Committee on National Resources and Public Works in this session.
The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) spoke about the government resorting to confrontation, bullying the provinces. It is interesting to note that throughout discussions leading to the ALCAN agreement which was negotiated last August and September not only with the government in Washington but also with the governments of the three western provinces, none of them of the same political stripe as the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), during negotiations for the largest private enterprise project in the history of Canada which will cost some $10 billion, there were no signs of any confrontation with the western premiers, of any bullying. Obviously if there ever was an issue with a potential for many conflicts, it is this project. Yet when I was in Alberta a few weeks ago, some of the Tory provincial members of parliament complimented me on the consultation which took place between the Prime Minister and the premier of that province during the discussions which took place leading up to the agreement with the U.S. government. So 1 think we have to take with a grain of salt what the Leader of the Opposition said about confrontation and bullying as the tactics of this government and realize that it is mostly political talk on his part. I think it is very appropriate, especially this week, after having watched the confrontation in the past year during which the Leader of the Opposition settled who will be the candidate for the Bow River riding, resorting to bullying and perhaps even revenge. It seems to me that if we really want to take the Leader of the Opposition seriously we must wonder how he would ever be able to run the country if he were to be prime minister when he cannot even look after the fights and defections in his own caucus.
As we go into this session of parliament and come to grips with the tremendous problems of the economy, unemployment, inflation and setting up new energy systems for our country, we will be facing an additional problem, that is the achievement of national unity in this country. At no time in our history have we had to face the same kind of challenge that the

October 27, 1977
The Address-Mr. Foster
federal government and this parliament will have to face in this session after the election of the separatist government in Quebec last fall.
It seems to me that the PQ government has moved rapidly in the course of the past year toward their primary aim of establishing a separate country. It seems to me that we will have to bring to bear every bit of wit and wisdom that we can muster in this place to meet this challenge in the next few months and in the next year or so. Certainly after reading the statements of the Leader of the Opposition, the leader of the NDP (Mr. Broadbent), and of the Prime Minister in this debate, I think there is no question about who is the party leader with the greatest understanding of this problem, the greatests appreciation of it, and the most ability. That is the Prime Minister.

I want to compliment the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) on his appointment in the last few months. He is a very courageous man to be taking such an important responsibility at a time when every world government faces such tremendous economic problems, problems of unemployment and of high inflation. Canada's problems in this regard are perhaps as great as are those of some of the other industrialized countries, but not as bad as those of many other countries. When one considers the growth that has taken place in the labour force in Canada as compared with other countries in the last eight or ten years, and our exposure to world inflation because of the high proportion of our gross national product being realized from trade, one realizes that this makes us more liable to encounter the very serious problems of unemployment and high inflation, but it does not lessen our responsibility to come to grips with them and to overcome them.
I believe the Minister of Finance in his speech faced these problems with candor, with courage and with honesty, speaking to the members of this House and to the Canadian people. He proposed important steps to overcome our problems and to improve our situation. He announced, for instance, a tax reduction of $100 for low income families, and geared it so that that reduction in taxes would come during January and February of this coming winter and so that it would provide a stimulus to the economy of some $700 million during that two month period, a period when consumer spending is often down. It should give a tremendous shot in the arm to consumer spending during that two month period.
The minister announced that the government will continue its program of restraint in spending. It has been indicated that the increase in government spending during the first half of 1977 was held at 5.2 per cent over 1976. That is even below the estimate of 7 per cent the President of the Treasury Board

(Mr. Andras) announced in his spending estimates last February.
The rate of increase in the civil service is being held at less than one per cent over last year. The minister announced the discontinuation of the Anti-Inflation Board as of April 14, 1978, so that both business and labour will know the plans of the government. This will create a great deal of certainty in the business community.
The Minister of Finance announced that a $150 million additional direct job creation fund would be provided for this coming winter. This is on top of the $450 million already announced this year. The minister also indicated that this level of spending for Canada Works would continue into next year, providing over $1 billion for direct job creation during the two-year period. This is important to the Algoma riding where there is persistently high seasonal unemployment because our construction industry is seasonal. During this coming winter we will be spending $1.8 million in the Algoma riding on Canada Works projects. Some 60 projects have now been approved. These projects will create over 500 jobs throughout the Algoma-Manitoulin area.
I certainly hope that some of the additional $150 million which is to be provided for direct job creation through the federal Labour Intensive Program will be provided to the small craft harbours branch. This is the branch of the Department of the Environment which provides marine facilities throughout our country. Surely with a negative balance in our tourism account with the United States we need to create the best possible tourist facilities we can to encourage our American friends to come and visit in Canada during the holiday season.
I was pleased that the Minister of Finance announced a $100 million incentive program to provide employment to private business. It seems to me that there is a limit to the amount of spending which can be done for direct job creation. We should be providing incentives to the private sector. Surely $100 million will provide a substantial incentive, and of course these jobs tend to be long lasting and permanent, whereas direct job creation jobs are not.
We all get very interesting letters from our constituents suggesting all kinds of projects and programs in which the government should be involved. I received one last week which suggested that we create a registered educational savings program which would operate similar to the registered retirement savings program or the registered home ownership program. Under this proposed program an employed person could put funds into a tax shelter during his high income working years. These funds would then be available to be withdrawn when that person wants to take advanced training in his own field. The money could be used to fund refresher courses in the person's present area of unemployment, or it could be used by a person training for a second career part way through his working life.
I have heard it said that persons being trained today should be prepared to change jobs at least three or four times during their active career. Surely that is true of politicians if not of the general population, but it seems to me that this proposal of
October 27, 1977

one of my constituents is a very good one. It would provide funds for this kind of retraining. The people themselves would be putting up the funds. It would not be put up by the government or by employers. People retraining for a year or so would not be in the labour force during that period. I certainly hope that the Minister of Finance will consider this suggestion in his next budget.
Yesterday I heard the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) speak in the House. I thought he made a very good speech, with all deference to the hon. member from the opposition who spoke just a few moments ago. I heard the minister mention that high on the list of priorities at the federal-provincial meetings which will be taking place in the next few weeks will be farm stabilization. I was glad to hear that because many sectors of Canadian agriculture, especially cow-calf operators, have gone through perhaps one of the most difficult periods ever in Canadian agricultural history during the past three years. I was encouraged that prices in Algoma-Manitoulin this year moved up somewhat, but cow-calf operators are still not getting a decent return for the work, the investment, and the management they provide to their farm operations. I hope that the stabilization will not be necessary as prices move up in the future, but surely we need to have a stronger and better program in place because of the cyclical nature of this industry.
The Minister of Agriculture also mentioned that he was prepared to bring in control legislation for imports of beef to maintain them at a reasonable level so that we do not get dumping on the Canadian market. I hope the minister will go ahead with this legislation. He indicated that he wanted some indication from the opposition that it would be prepared to support such legislation, and I hope that can be worked out.
In northern Ontario we were shocked last week at the announcement by INCO that it was planning to lay off some 2,800 people in the Sudbury district. That announcement not only affects the city of Sudbury but the entire district of Sudbury, much of which is in the eastern part of the Algoma riding. Some young workers who live in my constituency will be laid off by INCO.
To me it is almost unbelievable that a company as large and as important as INCO is to the Canadian economy would unilaterally make this decision without any consultation or without any notice to the government or to the labour unions involved. Surely this kind of action belongs to the dark ages of industrial relations and not in a modern industrial society. No responsible employer should lay off 2,800 workers in the dead of winter without prior consultation. All too often, and in too many communities in northern Ontario we have had to face this kind of situation in the past.
In Elliott Lake we faced this problem in the early 1960's when the United States government failed to pick up its option to purchase additional supplies of Canadian uranium. We saw the population of that community drop from around 25,000 to about 6,000 during those years, and the price of uranium dropped from about $13 a pound to about $4 or $5 a pound. The number of mines operating in that community dropped
The Address-Mr. McKenzie
from 13 to 2 during the 1960's. However, the federal government acted to save the town of Elliot Lake and the Township of Elliot Lake during those years. It decentralized the laboratories of the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources. It established the Elliot Lake Centre for Continuing Education in co-operation with the Ontario Department of Education. It established a program of uranium stockpiling which, during the 1960's, cost $100 million, and in the early 1970's cost $29 million. In the early 1970's it worked with other uranium producing countries to establish a floor price for export sales to maintain the mines and industry in communities like Elliot Lake and Uranium City.
Our Tory friends across the floor have often been critical of this action by the government. But if those mines had shut down in the early 1970's-as most would have-and had filled up with water and had to be pumped out and were just now starting into production, rather than being in full production and expanding in the last couple of years, what would the price of uranium be? It would certainly be much higher than $40 or $42 per pound.

Mr. Speaker, I have certainly looked forward to participating in this debate. Unfortunately, I cannot offer congratulations to the two members who moved the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne, as that would be hypocritical of me. 1 cannot congratulate anybody who is supporting and congratulating this government with its record. I look at these two members with disdain. It amazes me that they could get on their feet to support and praise this government.
I am very disappointed that the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner) left the Chamber because I have some very strong comments to make, both about his speech tonight and his past actions. I would have no hesitation about saying this to him if he were here. I will say it now, knowing that he reads Hansard every day and so will read my comments tomorrow. He is the Christine Jorgensen of the Canadian political scene. How anybody could do what he did, with his record of 19 years opposing the Liberals, is beyond comprehension. It is unbelievable the way he has spoiled himself.
The minister talked about a strong domestic climate. What a statement to come from him. I shall return to that in a moment. He gave some false information in this Chamber tonight about public hiring and said it is being restricted to 1 per cent. It is not 1 per cent at all, Mr. Speaker. Every cabinet minister is hiring through private employment agencies by the thousands and I have the figures to prove it. Also, every cabinet minister is hiring retired civil servants in the thousands on a contract basis. The amount for 1975-76 is $130 million. Yet they have the audacity to stand in this Chamber, and to

October 27, 1977
The Address-Mr. McKenzie
wander around the country saying they are restricting the growth of the civil service. I will have the rest of the figures before much longer, Mr. Speaker.
1 should like to comment now on the remarks made by the hon. member for Algoma (Mr. Foster) regarding the Bow River confrontation and the nominating meeting there. He tried to intimate that the Conservative party is the only party where there is a contest for a nomination. That is utter nonsense. I can remember St. Boniface in 1968 when the present member for that riding contested a cabinet minister. There was a kafuffle and they had to have two nominating meetings. I can remember a cabinet minister in Quebec in the same year who was challenged. He was defeated so he went to another riding, but he was defeated again. 1 remember another recent provincial Liberal nomination in Ontario where the leader of the Liberals had to rule things out of order and everything had to be done over again. There have been recent nominations in Manitoba where NDP cabinet ministers were contested. Let us not have this nonsense that the Conservative party is the only one that has contested nomination meetings. It is a lot of nonsense.

That is another one. They did not want his father here.
The hon. member for Algoma spoke of the $100 million incentive to business. That does not mean anything at all. The tax incentives are not going to keep business in Canada, and I shall go into more detail later. He spoke of mines closing. The mining industry has been driven out of this country with the double taxation. Between the Liberal government's involvement in taxing the mining industry, the former NDP government in Manitoba and the former Barrett government, mining has been driven out of the country. They are not going to go back and forth-once those companies are driven out, that is the end.
I have another comment about the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce who has become an apologist for the Liberal party. It is unbelievable to see him stand in this Chamber reading a speech. 1 remember when he was a constructive member of parliament and did not need a prepared speech. He knew how to give emphasis without reading a document prepared by some parliamentary assistant or whoever drafted it. The minister knows how I feel about him and 1 will say these things to his face tomorrow. Indeed, 1 have already done it. I have expressed my opinion on how I feel about the minister.
I want to get on now to economic issues, Mr. Speaker, as 1 do not like to express personal opinions but like to deal with facts. I should like to read some press comments on Canada's economic health.
A report of the OECD and World Bank states that Canada's standard of living has dropped to seventh place in the world compared to other nations. My colleagues tell me it has just dropped to ten-probably it will be twelfth tomorrow. A report in the Financial Times tells us that Canada's economy

lags still further behind the United States. Diane Cohn has reported that controls are now part of the inflation problem. The business section of the Winnipeg Free Press reports that Canadians are being ripped off by the GNP shortfall, and it is reported in the Globe and Mail that Canadians lead all foreigners in investing in the United States. This is something I want to comment upon tonight, Mr. Speaker.
This flow of capital to the United States will continue. In questions put to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) on July 19 in regard to this outflow of investment capital it was pointed out that Canadians are the number one investors in the United States. Mr. Speaker, this is an indication that they have absolutely no faith in Canada, and $100 million is not going to keep them here. In reply to a question put by the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) on that occasion, the Prime Minister replied:
As far as Canadian capital being invested elsewhere is concerned, there are no exchange controls on the Canadian dollar, and the Canadian investor is free to invest wherever he will get the maximum return for his dollar.
Who could argue with that, Mr. Speaker? What we want to know is what he is going to do to keep the investment dollar here. Apparently he is going to do absolutely nothing. I put a similar question to the great hon. Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce on October 19, and he replied:
I should like to thank the hon. member for the question. We enjoy in Canada complete freedom of investment and a free country.
Imagine the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce making a statement like that. He, who is supposed to attract industry to this country, says we are a great bunch of free enterprisers and if all business wants to move to the states and all investment money as well, that is fine. It is ironic, Mr. Speaker, because an article in a recent issue of Macleans magazine asks if Jack Horner is still his own man. Well, after the answer he gave me, Mr. Speaker, we know he is not his own man but, the article also asks-or Pierre Trudeau's? He is Pierre Trudeau's man now. They are both mouthing the same things-let all business and investment capital leave the country. What it is going to cost us will be very interesting to the Canadian people. I will get to that in a moment.
There are close to one and a half million people unemployed in Canada today. With this trend of investment money and businesses leaving, my prediction is that within four years there will be two and a half million people unemployed.
Today there are some 400,000 students graduating from schools, colleges, and universities each year, but we are creating only 200,000 new jobs yearly. By doing a little simple arithmetic, you will come up with your own figure; two million, three million.
What is it costing the Canadian public today to pay for UIC? Since 1973 it has cost the Government of Canada $4.8 billion over and above employee-employer contributions to keep the UIC fund solvent. That is the equivalent of $208 per man, woman and child in Canada. Since March, 1968, UIC
October 27, 1977

payments have amounted to $7.3 billion, or almost $800 per man, woman and child.
In the first six months of 1977 unemployment insurance benefits amounted to an average of $12.7 million per day, or $530,000 an hour, or $9,000 a minute, or $150 a second. That is something for the Canadian public to think about. They will not get any consolation from the comments of the Prime Minister or of the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce. They are great free enterprisers who will allow investment capital to go south of the line and allow businesses to move. They are such free enterprises they will not interfere in that transaction.
It is great to read articles like this in the paper:
N.Y. Woos Canadians in Ottawa
Eastern Ontario industrialists are being invited to a one-day seminar in Ottawa September 28 to be sold on the benefits of establishing branch plants in northern New York.
The seminar, organized by St. Lawrence County, is part of a stepped up effort by industry-craving communities along the south shore of the St. Lawrence Seaway to woo Canadian businessmen.
Isn't it encouraging to the Canadian taxpayer to read an article like that? A group of New York bankers have established a $500 million fund to assist Canadian businesses to move from Canada to the United States. Along the border states they are building business complexes to accommodate Canadian businesses. Once a trend like that starts, you do not stop it.
What is the government's alternative? It is putting up $450 million for make work and job creation projects on a temporary basis. Why does the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce not have a seminar to find out why these businesses are leaving? Why is he not doing something to keep them here? Never mind saying he is a great free enterpriser who will not do anything about it. He is one of the greatest trends the United States has ever had.
I wish to read some of the comments that have been made by Canadian businessmen. A spokesman for Jarry Electronics, which moved to Massena, New York, from Hawkesbury, Ontario, said:
Somewhere there's a point of no return and Canada is getting close to it.
A comment in the Ottawa Citizen on Canadian investment in the United States reads:
We didn't move just to get out of Canada-it was a matter of survival.
A Massey-Ferguson spokesman in the November 23, 1976, Toronto Globe and Mail stated:
The economic policy of the Trudeau government is frightening the business community into investing in the United States.
Here is another dandy from the July 23, 1977, Ottawa Citizen:
One hundred and forty Canadian manufacturing firms now have outlets in New York.
Don McGillivray of Southam News stated:
Canada is drifting along like a ship without a rudder.
The Address-Mr. McKenzie
An Ontario manufacturer commented:
Industries just can't survive in the current Canadian climate and many more will make the move to the U.S.
As I pointed out, this affects us. All we have to do is expand UIC and have these phony make-work projects. If the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce and this government were on their toes, they would be consulting with investment counsellors across Canada. This is something I have done. I recently consulted one in Winnipeg. He has a full-time profitable occupation assisting Canadian businesses move to the United States. This was mostly in Manitoba, but the political climate has improved there 100 per cent in the past two weeks.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all I would like to congratulate the hon. member for Louis-Hebert (Mr. Dawson) and the hon. member for Mal-peque (Mr. Wood) for their splendid contributions to this traditional debate. 1 take exception to the remarks of the hon. member who spoke before me. I think he is ill-mannered. He is aware of the tradition in this House of showing at least respect for the opinions of two newly arrived members in this House. He should at least have the dignity of showing them the respect they earned well.

Mr. Speaker, this debate represents one of the rare occasions for a member to speak of various subjects of particular interest to him. It is usually not partisan. Mr. Speaker, on October 10 last I concluded a two-year period as Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Urban Affairs. The experience has been rewarding. The many contacts made across the country, the speeches, the official visits, the work in committee and with the minister allowed me to better understand federal urban programs and to get closely involved in the housing policies and programs brought forth by this government to meet the expectations of Canadians in the area of urban planning and housing construction.
As 1 represent an entirely urban riding made up for a large part of neighbourhoods dating in many cases back over a hundred years, one of my major concerns has been working hard for the preservation of our architectural heritage and the rehabilitation of old neighbourhoods. That policy to restore and rehabilitate Ottawa-Vanier assured us of the preservation of our dear old neighbourhoods where a certain lifestyle has set in a long time ago and where tradition should play a part in shaping the face of the national capital so it may be reflected in Canada as a whole.
Housing in Ottawa-Vanier was substantially improved in the past four or five years. There is a great choice of alternatives. The programs under way, whether it be neighbourhood rehabilitation, construction or restoration, will continue to bring tangible benefits to my constituents.
The federal government has a substantial influence on urban Canada under the vast responsibilities that come under its jurisdiction. Every policy and every program initiated at the federal level in housing, transportation, immigration, economic assistance and others are felt in the final analysis at the local and surrounding community levels. That means that we, at the federal level, as well as our provincial counterparts, must always take into consideration the needs, the priorities and the cost problems, and continue to work closely with the municipal level and citizens committees to find the most practical solutions to the problems of urban planning and concentration.
There is also an important point that must be considered, at least at this time, and that is the fact that we do not have to accept trends unless we want to. All in all, trends largely reflect public behaviour patterns and the ways in which they are applied. Up to a point, those patterns can be reoriented and new patterns applied differently.
There are a number of federal levers that can serve in support of new objectives which reflect new values. For instance, the programs on housing, immigration, finance and the economy, transport and industry, regional development and many others. All those programs can give considerable support to provincial, regional and municipal development strategies in improving the quality of the urban environment.
One of the results of urban development and the concentration of populations has been the growth, at the periphery, of suburbs and dormitory towns. Around those concentration, commercial centres and job opportunities have developed. The riding of Ottawa-Vanier, downtown Ottawa, did not escape
October 27, 1977

the effects of the migration of its inhabitants to the outskirts. It slowed down the economic growth of downtown Ottawa, exerted strong pressures for new road systems linking the outskirts where people sleep to the heart of the city where people work.
Doubtless, a number of reasons explain the slowing down now apparent in yesterday's trends. A new awareness that brings it changing values, is probably another factor. The increasing number of persons formerly living in the suburbs or elsewhere now want to come back to live in the city. The change may not be dramatic but it does have salutary results. Now, people are asking that the quality of life in the city-core be better balanced between working and residential areas. That is a complete change-about with the trend of a few years ago. It is therefore important that any planning or strategy in the field of housing and urban renewal be closely tied in with those new trends.

Federal housing policies have had to be both progressive and responsive to the diversity of special needs that have always existed. This is at the heart of federal policies on shelter-not just to help provide houses of brick, mortar and wood-but to help people, particularly people who are unable to fend for themselves properly.
I am referring to people who make up important minorities in our society-the poor, the elderly, the sick, native people and others who are at a disadvantage in a competitive world. These have always been the first concern of a national housing policy, and today we are continuing to meet their needs through a variety of programs that are especially tailored to provide assistance while helping to retain the essential human dignity all people must possess. We don't do it alone, of course. There is an inter-dependence of governments in housing, as in most other important fields, and we work together to ensure that we are responding properly to the needs of people who are most vulnerable.
Obviously, we could not follow this path without the approval of the Canadian people, for the strength of the majority must be employed to help the vulnerable minorities. It is a credit to the people of this country that they so willingly support the principle that those of us who are blessed with good fortune have a fundamental responsibility toward our fellow-Canadians who need our help, whether temporarily or permanently. Call it a spirit of brotherhood, if you like, but it's there, it can be felt, and it contributes to the greatness of this huge country that sprawls from the Atlantic to the Pacific.
We have collectively been very preoccupied, and justifiably so, with building and improving our neighborhoods. We have developed flexible programs that fit our national needs and meet our national goals. All levels of government will continue no doubt to elaborate plans for improving the quality of life of all our neighborhoods.
Yet, we are faced, in Canada today, with a challenge of great importance to us all-the challenge of keeping this country together. Call it national unity or national understand-
The Address-Mr. J.-R. Gauthier ing, I, for one, prefer the term national understanding because I can better grasp its meaning.
To understand each other with all our regional and sectional loyalties, our varying customs and traditions; to understand what this country is all about with two official languages and a multitude of cultures; to understand that there are forces at work to build a better Canada while at the same time other forces that want to destroy it; therein lies the challenge! There is a threat or a crisis which menaces everything we have learned to love and cherish and that we so dearly want to keep. There is a far greater challenge ahead of us on the road to human brotherhood than we ever had to face before.
I was reminded recently of an old English proverb which says "do not trouble trouble till trouble troubles you." In my view, the only way to fight separatism is to make federalism a more attractive option.
History tells us that feelings of separatism were felt long ago in Canada. Lord Durham, one of our British governors, wrote in his report to England in the early 1800's: "I found two nations warring within the bosom of a single state".
History will tell you that Franco-Ontarians, and there are 500,000 of us in Ontario, had troubles in our fight to obtain the right to live in French in Ontario. We fought against regulations which forbade the use of French in Ontario schools. We fought to obtain primary and secondary French schools for our children, and finally obtained them in 1968.
We are still fighting for our right to use French in the courts of law of Ontario. We are asking for permission to draw up in French our wills, our contracts, our mortgages, and other ordinary legal documents. We are asking that essential services such as legal aid, health services, official government communications and documents be available in French, all things that most of you in this House take for granted in your provinces, be it in Quebec or elsewhere.
I could go on and give you a litany of services, such as permits, certificates, notices and requests for information, documents published by the Ontario ministries and government agencies, which are not available in French in Ontario. But those requests and concerns, as important as they are, all boil down to one basic principle called equality of opportunity.
1, and nearly a million other French speaking Canadians living outside Quebec, wish to be an active, respected, and wanted part of our country. We are Canadians. It so happens that we speak French in an English speaking milieu. Was not the idea of adopting two official languages, respectful of our individual heritages and traditional features, the purpose of creating a unified country in the first place? Surely the game plan is not for French to be balkanized to Quebec and for the rest of Canada to speak English? If it is, I will have no part of it. I want to feel at home in either language from coast to coast, everywhere in this country.

speechtext:
Hear, hear!

October 27, 1977
The Address-Mr. J.-R. Gauthier

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Unity to me does not mean uniformity. Neither does it mean that this society will develop into a uniform, regionalized or whatever you want system applicable all across the country. It has to be sensible, it has to be sensitive and respectful of all minorities, be they linguistic, social, cultural or economic. We all want individual recognition. We all want collective recognition. Minority groups are asking for recognition. That phenomenon is not peculiar to them or to anybody else; it is a phenomenon which we see when the provinces negotiate with the federal government, or when the municipalities negotiate with the provincial governments. What are we looking for, Mr. Speaker? We are looking for recognition. We are looking for recognition when this government negotiates with other countries. We are asking for recognition of our potential, recognition of our trade, of our cultural diversity, of our respect for human rights and of this great progressive democracy.
One unique feature about federalism is that it can adapt to circumstances. French-speaking minorities fear assimilation. If they do disappear through wilful neglect or indifference by the majority, these same majorities will in effect have contributed to separatism by attrition.
Separation of this country by attrition will come when no French is spoken outside Quebec and no English is spoken inside Quebec. Minorities, you see, can be disposed of in two ways. You attack them continuously or you ignore them completely. Both ways will surely kill them.
Rene Levesque, the premier of Quebec, is a well-known separatist. Lord Durham, in his way, was a separatist with a twist. Durham, in his now famous report to England, said about the French Canadians that the only solution to the problem was assimilation, and to that effect he proposed a plan. Are Francophone minorities outside Quebec the heirs of Lord Durham?
We have grown as a country as Canadians of both official languages moved about and established their neighbourhoods. If they had worked as hard on improving brotherhood as they have on building their neighbourhoods, we certainly would not be faced with the same problems facing us today. Some will tell us that national unity is threatened by the national economic problems or the social unrest caused by disturbing unemployment. I for one do not believe that you can separate economic, cultural or social problems when you talk of national understanding. You cannot speak of religion to a man who is hungry. You cannot speak of unity to the poor or the wanting. Let us not compartmentalize our society and its problems into parts that need to be fed, parts that need to be housed, parts that need to be transported, and so on. Let us look to the entire society, to the global problems we are presented with, so that the entire human being counts and prevails. Do not speak of social justice and equal opportunity equal to French-speaking minorities who in fact have had their rights trampled on for 110 years.
1 want to talk now about another grave problem facing my minority, the French-speaking minority outside Quebec, the problem of assimilation. The latest statistics, which are 1971,

indicate that 27 per cent of French-speaking minorities outside Quebec are being assimilated, and that is a very distressing rate. French outside Quebec, as a national language, is in the process of being relegated to the level of folklore in at least seven of our 10 provinces. Provincial bilingualism exists only in two provinces, Quebec and New Brunswick, although I must admit that Ontario is making some effort to adapt its policies to this challenge.
Where are we as a federation? Can we adapt to change? Right now, it seems to me, as a member of a linguistic minority, that the majority, be they French in Quebec or English outside Quebec, are reacting to their conscience while the minorities are gathering their punches to wake them up to reality. Those of us who are threatened are not at this time absent from this national debate. The minority linguistic groups will wage battle, for they have a country to lose and possibly a country to gain.
The fight will not take place between British Columbia and Quebec, or between Newfoundland and Quebec, or between any other provinces and Quebec; the fight for the minds, the hearts, and the allegiance of people will be at the national level. The results will most likely rest with the minority groups fighting prejudice, misunderstanding, and sometimes downright racism. The only way to fight the breakup of this country is to make federalism a more attractive option than separatism.
Canadians, regardless of their region, cultural roots, class or sex, only ask to be given the possibility of achieving relative equality. A sense of equity, freedom, and equality will have to be awakened in all Canadians. We can no longer continue to witness like helpless spectators the deterioration of the situation, the tearing to shreds of our national fabric.
English Canada will have to be perceived in its actions as being big enough to deal with Francophone groups on an equal footing, not based on the balance of numbers. It will have to be based on a definition of Canadian society tolerant and respectful of minorities, whether they are linguistic, cultural, social or economic minorities.
[ Translation]
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a few remarks on the comments pertaining to the Prime Minister's proposal last week in the Address in Reply, when he said that during this session he wanted to introduce in the House a bill on the referendum. Pending further details on that particular popular consultation formula, I would like the House to understand that it is urgent for all Canadians to realize that the time we have left to do the things we must do is getting shorter and shorter. I am convinced indeed that the date of the Quebec referendum is an important and meaningful date. I think, Mr. Speaker, that regardless of the results, the situation, if it is to change, must change in the meantime.
I do not know the date of the referendum proposed by the Parti Quebecois. I know that the results of that referendum could be highly disturbing. Should Quebecers vote negatively, shall we return to the status quo, to an attitude of the English-speaking majority saying that there is no problem,
October 27, 1977

that there is no need to worry because they will not separate? Or if the answer is yes, will we have a backlash of English opinion towards French-speaking minorities, to put it mildly? So it is very important, in the time available before this popular vote in Quebec, to focus on a federative solution which will really meet our expectations. The outcome will be a stronger Confederation.
President John F. Kennedy said this in his inaugural address:
Let us start all over again, remembering on both sides that courtesy is not a sign of weakness and that the proof of sincerity should always be established. Let us never be led by fear in our negotiations. And let us never fear to negotiate.
Mr. Speaker, may I call it ten o'clock?

subtopic: BILINGUALISM-SUGGESTED AMEN DMENT OF OFFICIAL LANGUAGES ACT TO ELIMINATE CERTAIN INJUSTICES
BILINGUALISM-SUGGESTED AMEN DMENT OF OFFICIAL LANGUAGES ACT TO ELIMINATE CERTAIN INJUSTICES
speechtext:
Last October 25, I asked a question of the Secretary of State to clear with him a very important matter. On September 30, the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras) announced the government's decision not to create bilingual districts. However, the Official Languages Act is mostly based on the creation of such bilingual districts. Is there then an alternative solution?
I asked the minister whether the government intends, in addition to the proposals which have been announced in the Speech from the Throne, to bring in amendments to the Official Languages Act during this session, thereby recognizing to that statute its supremacy in the field of linguistic equality over any other federal statute, thus correcting certain anomalies and inconsistencies that exist in some of the statutes.
In addition to the Official Languages Act, 1 could have mentioned, if I had had enough time, the Railway Act, the Winding-up Act and the Bank Act which contain all kind of vexatious measures from a linguistic standpoint. For instance, was it intended in the law and by the will of this Parliament to put restrictions on the issue of notices and announcements made by the railways to the public? I do not think so and I
Adjournment Motion
wish to explain further. Subsection (3) of section 243 of the Railway Act in particular now reads as follows:
Such notices shall, in the Province of Quebec, be written in the English and French languages, and, in the other provinces, in English.
This means that the right of the CN to make announcements in French in any province other than Quebec could be contested, which is contrary to the established practice and contrary, in my opinion, to the spirit of the law passed by this House.
There are a great number of other sections where such anomalies can be found. Last spring, 1 started reviewing the federal statutes dealing with the official languages and I noticed that amendments will have to be made to eliminate what I referred to, in my speech on national unity last July as "useless irritants".
After serious and in-depth examination of every statute, with the help of our legal counsel and a computer, as hon. members are aware, I prepared and today tabled a piece of legislation to bring some measure of fairness to our Canadian linguistic rights.
I noticed with very much pleasure, in the throne speech, that the government, after consulting with the provinces, will amend the Criminal Code to guarantee the right of the accused to be heard in the official language of his choice. But on the announcement that the government will not create bilingual districts, 1 felt we should have some alternative. Since the federal government have the Official Languages Act, since they are ready to meet with the provinces to amend the constitution by inserting a clause guaranteeing language equality across the country, it seems to me that the provinces should, as they may chose to do, follow in their own jurisdictions the federal lead.
I therefore have two goals. One, that the federal government recognize that the Official Languages Act has priority over every other statute of Canada, and second, that the provinces be encouraged to allow greater use of the official languages. Without discussing my bill any further, and to point out the degree of flexibility that is needed, it is essential that the provinces allow within their jurisdiction the use of both official languages. Briefly stated, my bill aims at asking permission. With a lot of good will, the provinces could allow this. I see no difficulty. There may be problems in some provinces where some may think that allowing means recognizing. For the time being I am not asking for official recognition, but for permission. If we here in Ontario were allowed legal documents in French, I would have them. 1 am not asking that the government officially declare themselves bilingual. I am simply asking this: Give me documents so that here, in Ontario, 1 may live in my mother tongue.
The time has come that we also allow a host of federal agencies to act within the spirit of the act, and in the case for instance of our railways that an end be put to the anomaly that prohibits announcements in French in provinces outside Quebec.

October 27, 1977
Adjournment Motion
In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, perhaps it would be advisable that the House move to international railway signs. Within a few months, if it is deemed advisable, a bill could be introduced for the adoption of international railway signs. That, Mr. Speaker, was basically my point. It is important that all these statutes be revised. I hope that the minister who will answer can give me a positive answer.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I indicated to the hon. member the other day, and as I announced earlier today in the House, it is the government's intention to bring forward amendments to the Official Languages Act. Our purpose will be to strengthen the law and particularly to strengthen the role of the parliamentary commissioner to enable him, in the context of parliament, to apply more effectively the objectives of the act.
I wanted to say as well that I am grateful to the hon. member for having brought to my attention, and to the attention of members, the inconsistencies and the anomalies which exist in several pieces of federal legislation. In doing so, I think he has performed an extremely valuable service for me and, I think, for other members of the House.
I agree strongly with the concerns he has expressed about some of the archaic provisions, and as a result of his representations I have asked my officials to be in touch with the Department of Justice and the Privy Council Office so that we can examine these statutes which he has drawn to our attention with a view to bringing forward necessary changes.
I have not yet had a chance to examine the legislation which he placed before the House today but I will certainly do so at the earliest opportunity, and I think we will find the kind of suggestions which he has made to be very helpful. It seems to me that he has demonstrated how one can effectively, as a member of parliament, serve the interest of the people one represents. His suggestions are extremely valuable and 1 intend to see that action is taken upon them.

subtopic: HOUSING-REASON FOR FAILURE TO PROTECT HOME BUYER
HOUSING-REASON FOR FAILURE TO PROTECT HOME BUYER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on October 20 at the first opportunity in this session I brought to the attention of the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) the plight of the residents of Bear Creek Park in Surrey, and I asked the following question of him:
Because of the indecent haste of the former minister in that portfolio to push AHOP programs, people, such as those in the Bear Creek estates, have been ripped off by fly-by-night contractors, as 1 have discussed with the minister on numerous occasions, and by the government directive that housing inspectors inspect only for the security of the money lenders, while the home buyer is left out in the cold. I would like to know why there was nothing about housing in the Speech from the Throne and why there is no protection for the home buyer.
The minister's answer was to the effect that he is sorry for the mistakes, he hopes there will be no such mistakes in the future, and that is where it ended. This was an admission of failure by the minister and the officials of his department, and

a refusal to accept any responsibility for what happened in the Bear Creek estates.
I want to assure the minister that I am not talking about the program itself because I know, now that the program has been in effect for two or three years, there are some fine AHOP projects that have been produced by very reputable contractors. I am not talking about the program itself. What 1 am talking about is at least one example, which can be multiplied across Canada, where people who had put their trust in a government program have been ripped off because of the sloppy administration by government administrators.
The problem is one of the minister, wanting to push the program to such a degree so as to have statistics to show that the program was a great success, and in his interest to have good statistics on housing starts he allowed his departmental officials, and perhaps even pushed them, to bring in all kinds of contractors on stream who could not be trusted as people with a good reputation so far as the quality of housing they would provide was concerned. I would like to outline briefly what has happened.
In this particular case 95 per cent of the homes were bought by the buyers from the contractor on the basis of plans presented. In the process of the building of those homes the contractor took it upon himself to change the plans, and when the buyers would view the houses as the plans were being changed, they would demur and object. The contractor would say that in the end things would turn out and that the buyers would be happy with the end product. But the end product was so shoddy that all the residents got together to object to what happened.
I showed the minister pictures of the substandard housing which was provided in the end for the full price of the AHOP project, and he himself was shocked. I know he was concerned about this.
The important fact is that the CMHC officials in Vancouver were pointedly asked by the residents and the buyers of Bear Creek estates not to make the final payment to the contractor, but they were totally ignored. The contractor got his money. He took off, and the buyers were left sitting high and dry. Actually, I should not say that because there were water problems, moisture, condensation, back-flow and water coming in the doors.
I should take a few minutes to read about some of the problems. The inspectors came back, looked, and admitted that their inspections had not been adequate. For example, there was deterioration because of moisture build-up in the windows. The doors were installed, but the weather stripping directed water into the houses instead of out of them. Not only was there shoddy workmanship; there were also violations of the code. The administrator from Vancouver signed a statement saying that a building did not meet section 35(B)(4) of the residential standards of CMHC. In another one the lighting fixtures did not meet section 35(B) of the residential standards. These are direct violations of the code. The inspec-

tors let these violations go, and the people had to pay full price. Now they are stuck.
The minister did show interest and was genuinely concerned about what happened, but the coup de grace is that in the end he said that it was too bad this happened but that perhaps these people should look for legal help for redress of their grievances. That contractor is long gone. He has closed down that company. He has no doubt vacuumed the company's bank account. There is not a thing these people can get, and they are stuck.
Departmental brochure NHA 5128-15 says:
The inspection routines are designed to make sure that the completed house will be adequate security for the NHA mortgage loan.
I wonder if Royal Trust and Montreal Trust have enough money somewhere to hire their own inspectors. Does CMHC have to carry out inspections to make sure the mortgage loans are protected? Mr. Speaker, in assuming my responsibilities as Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Urban Affairs 1 am pleased to provide the House with additional comments on the role of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation in the construction of houses in the Bear Creek Park Subdivision. As the hon. member is aware, my minister has maintained a keen personal interest in this matter; to wit, the meetings he has had to which the hon. member referred.
The hon. member made reference to the Speech from the Throne and, as mentioned by my minister a few days ago, if all the items with respect to AHOP, housing, and all the other aspects of the ministries of this government were included in the Speech from the Throne, the Queen would still be here in Ottawa.

speechtext:
With all due respect I believe that there may be some misundertanding on the part of the hon. member for
Adjournment Motion
Surrey-White Rock (Mr. Friesen) about the type of protection that CMHC provides for AHOP purchasers. All AHOP homes are inspected regularly by CMHC during construction. They must be in reasonable conformity with approved plans, and they must meet minimum standards of construction.
When owners of the Bear Creek Park houses indicated that they were not satisfied with the construction of their homes, CMHC met repeatedly with them and the builder to help resolve the problems. It is important to note, Mr. Speaker, that CMHC was successful in having the builder return to correct certain items necessary to bring the units up to the standards. The corporation was also able to encourage the builder to correct a number of other items that met standards, but the corporation went beyond that in meeting the standards to encourage the builder to maintain his workmanship to the owners' satisfaction.
The units now meet construction standards. However, the workmanship itself may not be up to the expectations of some purchasers, and this appears to be the major source of their continuing dissatisfaction. Moreover, strained relations between the builder and some of the home owners contributed to a hardening of attitudes on both sides, and CMHC spent a great deal of time trying to mediate these disputes.
One of the main difficulties here, Mr. Speaker, is the disparity between the purchasers' expectations regarding modest housing and the final product. Unfortunately this situation tends to arise when purchasers select their homes from plans or models. Differences between these and the actual home they buy are a source of disappointment and frustration, even though their house is in reasonable conformity with the plans from which the units were chosen.
The builder has advised CMHC that he is not prepared to do any more work on the houses-which now meet standards-and he is no longer active in the construction industry. I sympathize with the home owners, Mr. Speaker, but there is no question that CMHC did everything it possibly could within its mandate to help the home owners, as it does in every case. It was to help purchasers such as these that previous ministers of state for urban affairs, as well as the present minister in his former capacity as minister of consumer and corporate affairs, sought the creation of a national consumer warranty plan for new home buyers. Warranty programs are now being implemented by most provincial governments, and consumers can look forward to an improved level of protection. The minister attaches a great deal of importance to working with HUDAC and the provinces to ensure that all Canadians receive equal protection.

VETERANS AFFAIRS-AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR WIDOWS OF VETERANS RECEIVING LESS THAN 48 PER CENT DISABILITY PENSION-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was wondering who was going to reply for the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. MacDonald) but I see we

October 27, 1977
Adjournment Motion
have one Liberal left. Mr. Speaker, if one were to count the times the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) and I have brought up the topic I will raise tonight, I am sure we would lead the parade in bringing to light examples of inequities against Canadians. I brought up two questions yesterday. One concerned widows' pensions, and one was to the effect that veterans are falling behind in disability pensions as compared to their counterparts in the public service.
I do not understand how anybody can fail to see the discrimination that exists in veterans legislation. A veteran receiving a 48 per cent disability pension will leave a pension to his widow when he dies. If he receives 1 per cent less, however, which amounts to about $203 per year, she will not receive anything when he dies. Unless his death is attributable to his war days, she is left high and dry. She must resort to welfare. Canadians are saying to that woman, who probably spent many hours caring for her husband before he died, "You look after yourself, dear". The funny thing is there is now a way to correct that in the legislation. It has been brought to the attention of the minister on a number of occasions. It has to do with War Veterans Allowance recipients.
A War Veterans Allowance recipient receives somewhere in the vicinity of $487. He is probably equal to a disability pensioner at 65 or 70. If he dies, his wife is protected for one year at the married rate. After the year, she reverts to the single rate. However, she does have that built-in protection. The disability pensioner suffering from war wounds does not have that same advantage.
The other anomaly is the fact that the disability pensioner at only 5 per cent can qualify for War Veterans Allowance and probably get $400. His wife is protected. Someone receiving a disability pension of less than 47 per cent is better off to apply for War Veterans Allowance. This anomaly in the legislation has to be corrected. However, the government will not listen.
The other question I brought to the attention of the minister was with regard to the basic rate of pension and the indexing of that. After many years of fighting and hollering, we were able to establish a category on which to base the basic rate of pension for the disability pensioner. It was finally based by a tripartite committee on the average salary of the five lowest categories in the public service.
As a result, the one on disability indexed according to the cost of living increase is falling behind the rate of the public servant at $536 each year. The minister agrees that is wrong and has to be corrected. However, yesterday he made the ridiculous statement that they are only going to give them half the cost of living index and that veterans, as good Canadians, will accept that. They are good citizens all right. They were good Canadians 60 years ago when they went overseas as youngsters on behalf of Canada. Some sacrificed their lives. Some who came back were maimed and disabled.
Finally, after 50 years we had this basic rate established. They have now fallen behind and nobody will listen. I ask the

parliamentary secretary, how long do they have to wait? There are only 12,404 World War I disability pensioners left. They will all be gone, God forbid, in two or three years. To deny them the benefit of a commitment made by Canadian governments over 60 years is, to my mind, a blot on our society.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as Armistice Day draws near it is certainly a privilege for me to answer in place of the Parliamentary Secretary for Veterans Affairs (Mr. Parent).
When the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. MacDonald) answered the question asked by the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe (Mr. Marshall) yesterday it was with regret that he had to say that the government has looked seriously at the question of a possible increase to the basic rate of pension payable for death or disability related to military service, but had decided not to increase the pension at this time. Hon. members will appreciate that at this time of financial restraint additional funds over and above the normal increases which will be made in January, 1978, are not currently available.
Even though it cannot provide an additional increase, I should at the same time point out that this government has had the veterans very much in mind over the years. As an example, in January, 1971, the rate of pension for a veterans whose pensioned disabilities were assessed at 100 per cent, and who was unmarried with no dependants, was $265. A 10 per cent increase was granted on 1 April, 1971, to bring the rate to $292 a month. Indexing of pensions was instituted so that effective 1 January, 1972, the rate has been changed annually in accordance with the consumer price index. In addition there was a substantial 24 per cent increase in mid-1972, following on the study and recommendations of the joint study group.
As a result I am able to announce that the basic rate of pension will increase by 7.2 per cent effective 1 January, 1978, so that as of that date the unmarried 100 per cent pensioner will receive $596.70 a month. A married 100 per cent pensioner with one child will get $823.52. A widow without children will receive $447.53, and if she has two dependent children she will receive $716.06.
Insofar as the pro rata pension to widows of pensioned veterans is concerned. 1 have very little to add since a statement was last made on this subject.
The suggestion has been made that a widow should receive a pro rata pension if her husband had been in receipt of a disability pension of 47 per cent or less. This is because she would be fully pensionable as a widow if his pension had been 48 per cent or more at the time of death. What is sometimes missed is that the widow will be pensioned if her husband's death occurred during wartime or was attributable to his service, regardless of the degree of the assessment of his disability. The question which arises is whether, if death was not in any way attributable to military service, a widow's pension should be paid because of the service connection.
October 27, 1977

We know that the benefits provided to the disabled serviceman or woman, or to their surviving dependants, are far greater than those provided by most other countries. I am not aware of any of our major western wartime allies who pay
Adjournment Motion
automatic survivor benefits to widows approaching the 48 per cent basis which we in Canada use.
